title: Aukus is ‘worst, riskiest and most costly’ Australian defence decision ever, public inquiry into submarine deal says
content_c:
A public inquiry into the $368bn Aukus nuclear submarine agreement has called the plan “the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever made by an Australian government”, urging its immediate termination.
Former Labor MP and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett and former chief of defence Adm Chris Barrie led the inquiry dominated by critics of the deal with the UK and US, recommending the suspension of plans for new bases and for a royal commission to be held into the agreement signed by the former Morrison government.
Its report, titled Surrendering Australia: the Aukus Deception, says Australia risks being dragged into military conflict with China because of the presence of powerful nuclear submarines. Aukus badly undermines Australia’s sovereignty and undercuts longstanding commitments to nuclear non-proliferation, it says.
The report calls for a rework of the second pillar of the agreement, which covers technology and defence capability sharing, and for a fundamental recalibration of Australia’s relationship with Beijing.
After hearings around the country and more than 1,000 public submissions, the inquiry highlighted a lack of scrutiny and oversight over the five years since Aukus was announced and called for the auditor general and federal parliament to launch independent reviews.
“Since coming to power, Labor has failed to conduct a thorough review of this most significant of defence agreements,” Garrett told the National Press Club in Canberra.
“Conceived in secret, Aukus has spurned established defence and parliamentary oversight practices.”
He said the Stirling defence precinct in Perth risked becoming a “de facto US base” hosting as many as 2,000 serving American personnel, and that nearby communities including Rockingham and Fremantle would become targets for attack.
“The Aukus submarine plan is not tenable,” Barrie, who served as chief of defence between 1998 and 2002, said.
“It’s time for our government to take the lead on this matter. Scrap the Aukus submarine plan now, and rebuild national security decision-making processes.”
Labor agreed to support the deal for Australia to acquire nuclear submarines, which was negotiated under Morrison, then US president Joe Biden and UK prime minister Boris Johnson. As part of the agreement, Australia is funding upgrades to the US defence industrial base and is due to start receiving secondhand Virginia class nuclear submarines around 2032.
But delays and cost blowouts for production of submarines for the US Navy have led to scepticism that Australia will receive the in-service boats.
The UK parliament held a year-long review and, after an inquiry by the Pentagon in 2025, Donald Trump agreed to support Aukus.
But former prime ministers Paul Keating and Malcolm Turnbull, former foreign affairs ministers Gareth Evans and Bob Carr, environmental and security campaigners, and some within Labor believe Aukus is not in Australia’s national interest.
Garrett warned any certainty the US president would eventually agree to send submarines to Australia could not be guaranteed.
“There are no refunds, no enforceable obligations on partner countries, and no recourse if things go wrong,” he said.
The inquiry estimates an additional $180bn will be needed to deal with nuclear waste because of Aukus.
Australia has not identified a permanent storage site for the nuclear waste generated by the submarine fleet, including the high-level radioactive waste from the reactor core and spent fuel, which will remain toxic for thousands of years.
The government’s preferred measure of the total cost of the deal is 0.15% of GDP over its lifetime.
The first Virginia-class nuclear sub from the US is due to arrive in Australia in 2032, with another arriving every four years, before the Australian-built model is ready for operations. The bespoke SSN Aukus model is due to come online in 2042.

title: King tells Commonwealth leaders that Britain’s role in slave trade was ‘shameful’ but stops short of apology – as it happened
content_c:
The King has told Commonwealth leaders the transatlantic slave trade “fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow”, but did not offer an apology. As the Press Association reports, in his address to presidents and prime ministers, Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to “address the wrongs of the past with action for the future”. He delivered his speech against the background of Andy Burnham announcing a change in long-established government policy and making an offer of talks on a slavery apology but not financial reparations. The King told the leaders of the Commonwealth’s 56 member states meeting in Antigua:
Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.
And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.
The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future.
Here is John Crace’s sketch of Kemi Badenoch’s speech and Q&A with journalists this morning.
And this is how it starts.
HMS Wellington. A decommissioned Grimsby-class sloop from the second world war. A warship that has been moored on the Thames, going nowhere for the best part of 80 years. Today’s venue for the leader of the opposition to explain why the Conservative party hollowed out defence spending throughout their time in office. Sorry. Scrub that. To welcome in a brave new world order. Come aboard the good ship Badenoch. There are times when you wonder if the Tory media team have been infiltrated by Labour HQ. Still, we might as well enjoy it while we can.
Burnham claims Badenoch 'misreading public mood' in her opposition to negotiating new relationship with EU
Andy Burnham has accused critics of his proposed new trade deal with the EU of “misreading the public mood”.
As the Guardian reports, a deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products has now been agreed. At a summit in Brussels later this month, the EU and the UK will also be discussing deals covering emissions trading and youth mobility.
Speaking to reporters this morning, Kemi Badenoch said she could not say whether or not she would back the deal covering food products because she had not seen the detail. (See 10.38am.) And she said she was not opposed to a renegotiation per se, because she thought the EU-UK trade relationship needed “constant negotiating”.
But she also said she thought any proposal from Burnham was likely “to make things worse, not better”, and she said dynamic alignment with the EU on regulation was a “red line” that would be unacceptable to the Tories. As the Guardian report says, the deal that has been agreed does require dynamic alignment on sanitary and phytosanitary regulation.
Burnham said that the Treasury had confirmed in recent days that agreements under negotiation ahead of a summit later this month could raise GDP by 0.4% – up from the previous estimate of 0.3%.
And, in an interview with The Economist, he also hit back at Badenoch for criticising his attempts to forge a new relationship with the EU. He said:
I think it’s interesting because I sense, since conference, that there is an appetite to discuss it. And those who are making the argument over ‘Oh my goodness, don’t open up this psychodrama’ are misreading the public mood in my view.
Referring to the economic benefits of the deal being discussed at the summit later this month, he said:
A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now, that is a number that you cannot ignore.
The British and Australian governments have backed a joint agreement at the Commonwealth summit on working together to tackle threats directed at parliamentarians, especially women. Here is an extract.
We commit to working together with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, with the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians, and with countries from across the Commonwealth to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse and support democratic participation across the Commonwealth. We’ll hold the first forum in 2027 and will engage all those in the Commonwealth who share these values.
There are a range of software tools that are being trialled in our parliaments and around the world, and we welcome and encourage this innovation.
While we work to change attitudes, restore respectful debate and return people’s choice, in the short term we can commit to take steps together to protect our democracies.
MSPs call for review of law allowing people with just temporary rights to be living in Scotland to be elected to Holyrood
Severin Carrell
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
MSPs at Holyrood have called on Scottish ministers to review a law which allowed the Indian-born student Q Manivannan to win a seat at Holyrood in May, claiming public confidence in parliament was “fragile”.
The standards, procedures and public appointments committee said in a report that the rationale for allowing people with limited rights to be in the UK was “simply not clear” and had “run ahead of what the public want”.
Under the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025, overseas citizens with the legal right to live in Scotland can stand for Holyrood and local councils, even if their rights are temporary.
There was an outcry led by the Conservatives and Reform UK in May when Manivannan was elected as a Scottish Greens list MSP for Edinburgh and Lothians East. A successful PhD candidate at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, giving them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Jenny Minto, the Scottish National party MSP who chairs the committee, and who voted in favour of the reforms last year, said public sentiment appears to have swung against the policy. She said:
It is vital that Scotland has elected representatives who look like the communities they represent. This diversity helps build trust in our elected institutions.
But we know that this trust is fragile, and so careful consideration needs to be given to all electoral reform that comes before us.
Reform UK was delighted by the committee’s recommendation, which follows proposals by ministers to extend the right to Commonwealth citizens, but the Scottish Greens said it was regressive. The Scottish Greens said:
There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.
MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convenor and deputy convenor of the committee. It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment.
Burnham claims he cares less about criticism from newspapers than previous PMs did
Andy Burnham has said that he cares less about what the newspapers say about him than previous prime ministers did.
In one of his interviews with Daniel Hewitt for the ITV documentary being shown tonight about his first 100 days in office, Burnham was asked if he cared less about what papers like the Daily Mail and the Sun said about him than some of his predecessors did. Burnham replied: “Definitely.”
He said:
I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there and then the whole world [being] meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that anymore.
Burnham also defended prioritising social media more instead. He said:
People want more involvement, more understanding of the way politics is being done and that’s what I’m bringing. And hopefully it connects with people, particularly younger people, who may have felt quite distant from politics.
In another interview for the programme, Burnham rejected the suggestion that he was ruthless. Explaining why he did not like the description, he said:
Determined, I definitely would say that [I am] determined. I will come back and back and back at something. I’ve always been like that. Ruthless to me says you just have a disregard for everybody else. And that wouldn’t be me. But I am determined.
Burnham also revealed that, since becoming PM, he continues to go running regularly – and that this is often when his “best thoughts” occur. He explained:
If you’re asking me about what’s the thing that makes it work, I go running and I’ve not stopped my running. It’s when my mind goes a bit into neutral. And I feel then I get my best thoughts in those moments.
You know, all of a sudden, "Oh, that, yeah, I’ll do that.’ Or a particularly intractable problem that you’ve been thinking and worrying about – all of a sudden, I’ve been out on a run sometimes, and you just think, ‘Ah, that’s the way I’ll go into that one.’
Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences
Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child, Peter Walker reports.
Charles ended his speech urging Commonwealth leaders to “recommit … to a Commonwealth in which our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose”.
Charles said he was glad climate proposals were being considered at Chogm.
Here in the Caribbean, as in so many parts of our Commonwealth, climate change is not some distant prospect. It is an alarming reality.
As we know, large ocean states have contributed little to the causes of climate change, and yet they are among those bearing the greatest cost.
If we mobilise climate finance through the private sector and with the leveraging capacity of the public sector, we can drive investment into climate resilience.
Nature herself is an essential form of capital that sustains our prosperity and well-being. And yet we have persisted for too long to live off nature’s capital, rather than her income.
To restore nature is therefore not to choose our environment over our economy. It is to invest in the very foundations of our economy, not to mention our security.
Charles said Commonwealth values have never been more important.
What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values of democracy and the rule of law, of respect, equal dignity and human rights, of sustainable development, of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts, and they guide us to action.

It’s not out there apologising.The purpose of the apology is to make us look weak. It is to make this country look weak. And once we start looking weak, then we have every man and his dog making demands and sending us an invoice, which the British taxpayer has to pay. Continue reading...

As the Press Association reports, in his address to presidents and prime ministers, Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to “address the wrongs of the past with action for the future”. He delivered his speech against the background of Andy Burnham announcing a change in long-established government policy and making an offer of talks on a slavery apology but not financial reparations. The King told the leaders of the Commonwealth’s 56 member states meeting in Antigua:
Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past.
The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.
And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.
The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future.
Here is John Crace’s sketch of Kemi Badenoch’s speech and Q&A with journalists this morning.
And this is how it starts.
HMS Wellington. A decommissioned Grimsby-class sloop from the second world war. A warship that has been moored on the Thames, going nowhere for the best part of 80 years. Today’s venue for the leader of the opposition to explain why the Conservative party hollowed out defence spending throughout their time in office. Sorry. Scrub that. To welcome in a brave new world order. Come aboard the good ship Badenoch. There are times when you wonder if the Tory media team have been infiltrated by Labour HQ. Still, we might as well enjoy it while we can.
Burnham claims Badenoch 'misreading public mood' in her opposition to negotiating new relationship with EU
Andy Burnham has accused critics of his proposed new trade deal with the EU of “misreading the public mood”.
As the Guardian reports, a deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products has now been agreed. At a summit in Brussels later this month, the EU and the UK will also be discussing deals covering emissions trading and youth mobility.
Speaking to reporters this morning, Kemi Badenoch said she could not say whether or not she would back the deal covering food products because she had not seen the detail. (See 10.38am.) And she said she was not opposed to a renegotiation per se, because she thought the EU-UK trade relationship needed “constant negotiating”.
But she also said she thought any proposal from Burnham was likely “to make things worse, not better”, and she said dynamic alignment with the EU on regulation was a “red line” that would be unacceptable to the Tories. As the Guardian report says, the deal that has been agreed does require dynamic alignment on sanitary and phytosanitary regulation.
Burnham said that the Treasury had confirmed in recent days that agreements under negotiation ahead of a summit later this month could raise GDP by 0.4% – up from the previous estimate of 0.3%.
And, in an interview with The Economist, he also hit back at Badenoch for criticising his attempts to forge a new relationship with the EU. He said:
I think it’s interesting because I sense, since conference, that there is an appetite to discuss it. And those who are making the argument over ‘Oh my goodness, don’t open up this psychodrama’ are misreading the public mood in my view.
Referring to the economic benefits of the deal being discussed at the summit later this month, he said:
A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now, that is a number that you cannot ignore.
The British and Australian governments have backed a joint agreement at the Commonwealth summit on working together to tackle threats directed at parliamentarians, especially women. Here is an extract.
We commit to working together with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, with the Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians, and with countries from across the Commonwealth to bring together technology, expertise and practical solutions to help protect parliamentarians from online abuse and support democratic participation across the Commonwealth. We’ll hold the first forum in 2027 and will engage all those in the Commonwealth who share these values.
There are a range of software tools that are being trialled in our parliaments and around the world, and we welcome and encourage this innovation.
While we work to change attitudes, restore respectful debate and return people’s choice, in the short term we can commit to take steps together to protect our democracies.
MSPs call for review of law allowing people with just temporary rights to be living in Scotland to be elected to Holyrood
Severin Carrell
Severin Carrell is the Guardian’s Scotland editor.
MSPs at Holyrood have called on Scottish ministers to review a law which allowed the Indian-born student Q Manivannan to win a seat at Holyrood in May, claiming public confidence in parliament was “fragile”.
The standards, procedures and public appointments committee said in a report that the rationale for allowing people with limited rights to be in the UK was “simply not clear” and had “run ahead of what the public want”.
Under the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025, overseas citizens with the legal right to live in Scotland can stand for Holyrood and local councils, even if their rights are temporary.
There was an outcry led by the Conservatives and Reform UK in May when Manivannan was elected as a Scottish Greens list MSP for Edinburgh and Lothians East. A successful PhD candidate at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, giving them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Jenny Minto, the Scottish National party MSP who chairs the committee, and who voted in favour of the reforms last year, said public sentiment appears to have swung against the policy. She said:
It is vital that Scotland has elected representatives who look like the communities they represent. This diversity helps build trust in our elected institutions.
But we know that this trust is fragile, and so careful consideration needs to be given to all electoral reform that comes before us.
Reform UK was delighted by the committee’s recommendation, which follows proposals by ministers to extend the right to Commonwealth citizens, but the Scottish Greens said it was regressive. The Scottish Greens said:
There are thousands of people with limited leave to remain who live and work in Scotland and have made a home here, including Commonwealth citizens. They should be able to stand for our parliament and councils.
MSPs backed this change unanimously at the time, including the convenor and deputy convenor of the committee. It would be a regrettable backwards step for representation and democracy if Scotland was to roll back on this commitment.
Burnham claims he cares less about criticism from newspapers than previous PMs did
Andy Burnham has said that he cares less about what the newspapers say about him than previous prime ministers did.
In one of his interviews with Daniel Hewitt for the ITV documentary being shown tonight about his first 100 days in office, Burnham was asked if he cared less about what papers like the Daily Mail and the Sun said about him than some of his predecessors did. Burnham replied: “Definitely.”
He said:
I left Westminster for a reason. I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there and then the whole world [being] meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that anymore.
Burnham also defended prioritising social media more instead. He said:
People want more involvement, more understanding of the way politics is being done and that’s what I’m bringing. And hopefully it connects with people, particularly younger people, who may have felt quite distant from politics.
In another interview for the programme, Burnham rejected the suggestion that he was ruthless. Explaining why he did not like the description, he said:
Determined, I definitely would say that [I am] determined. I will come back and back and back at something. I’ve always been like that. Ruthless to me says you just have a disregard for everybody else. And that wouldn’t be me. But I am determined.
Burnham also revealed that, since becoming PM, he continues to go running regularly – and that this is often when his “best thoughts” occur. He explained:
If you’re asking me about what’s the thing that makes it work, I go running and I’ve not stopped my running. It’s when my mind goes a bit into neutral. And I feel then I get my best thoughts in those moments.
You know, all of a sudden, "Oh, that, yeah, I’ll do that.’ Or a particularly intractable problem that you’ve been thinking and worrying about – all of a sudden, I’ve been out on a run sometimes, and you just think, ‘Ah, that’s the way I’ll go into that one.’
Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences
Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child, Peter Walker reports.
Charles ended his speech urging Commonwealth leaders to “recommit … to a Commonwealth in which our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose”.
Charles said he was glad climate proposals were being considered at Chogm.
Here in the Caribbean, as in so many parts of our Commonwealth, climate change is not some distant prospect. It is an alarming reality.
As we know, large ocean states have contributed little to the causes of climate change, and yet they are among those bearing the greatest cost.
If we mobilise climate finance through the private sector and with the leveraging capacity of the public sector, we can drive investment into climate resilience.
Nature herself is an essential form of capital that sustains our prosperity and well-being. And yet we have persisted for too long to live off nature’s capital, rather than her income.
To restore nature is therefore not to choose our environment over our economy. It is to invest in the very foundations of our economy, not to mention our security.
Charles said Commonwealth values have never been more important.
What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values of democracy and the rule of law, of respect, equal dignity and human rights, of sustainable development, of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts, and they guide us to action.

title: Spain transport minister offers resignation in wake of train accident
content_c:
Spain transport minister offers resignation in wake of train accident
November 3, 2026
Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente offered his resignation on Tuesday in the wake of one of Europe's worst rail disasters in recent memory last week that killed 69 people.
The tragedy, Spain's second fatal rail collision in less than a year, has intensified scrutiny of railway safety and added political pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez ahead of parliamentary elections on November 29.
In January, a train crash in the southern Andalusia region killed 46 people.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot continue in office with two accidents of this severity in less than a year," he told lawmakers while announcing his intention to resign.
Puente, member of Sanchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, also said he would withdraw his name from the list of parliamentary electioncandidates. He did not specify when he would leave his post.
Puente's political opponents had demanded he step down, while train unions had been unhappy with him for appearing to pin blame for the disaster on one rail control center operator.
Government unveils new rail safety measures
Just hours before addressing lawmakers, Puente had presented improved rail network safety measures and told a press conference the government would "work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public's trust in high-speed rail."
This included plans for control center software that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot traffic anomalies, and an AI agent for system oversight to "minimize the possibility of human error."
Another measure Puente mentioned was requiring a second operator confirm decisions made in scenarios involving a faulty automatic safety system.
The accident happened during the failure of an automated safety system that had stopped all trains along a 63-kilometer stretch of track between Madrid and Seville on Wednesday morning.
Despite the stoppage on the line, a control center allowed a high-speed train operated by state-owned rail company Renfe to continue its journey.
The Renfe train collided with stopped train owned by private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda in Toledo province.

title: US-Zwischenwahlen: Demokraten steuern auf Wahlerfolg zu
content_c:
Trend bei US-Zwischenwahlen Demokraten steuern auf Wahlerfolg zu
Nach Schließung vieler Wahllokale zeichnet sich ein Erfolg für die Demokraten ab. Laut US-Medien ist klar, dass sie vier Senatssitze von den Republikanern erobern. Auch im Rennen um die Mehrheit im Repräsentantenhaus machen sie wichtige Punkte.
Bei den Zwischenwahlen in den USA deuten sich einige wichtige Erfolge für die Demokraten an. Dies berichten übereinstimmend US-Medien auf Grundlage von Nachwahlbefragungen und ersten Auszählungsergebnissen.
Demokraten können mit Mehrheit im Repräsentantenhaus rechnen
Vor der Wahl war damit gerechnet worden, dass die Demokraten den Republikanern die Mehrheit im Repräsentantenhaus abnehmen können. Es gibt nun konkrete Hinweise, dass es tatsächlich dazu kommen könnte.
Nach Prognosen der Nachrichtenagentur AP gehen mehrere Sitze an die Demokraten, die bisher von den Republikanern gehalten wurden. Demnach erlangte etwa in einem Wahlkreis im Bundesstaat North Carolina die Demokratin Jamie Ager einen Sitz, der zuvor republikanisch besetzt war.
Im US-Bundesstaat New Jersey wird die Demokratin Rebecca Bennett den republikanischen Kongressabgeordneten Tom Kean ablösen. Die frühere Soldatin setzte sich gegen den Abgeordneten durch, der bereits zwei Amtszeiten im Repräsentantenhaus saß. Der Wahlbezirk wechselte bei den beiden vorangegangenen Zwischenwahlen jeweils die Partei und galt deshalb auch diesmal als umkämpft.
Im Bundesstaat Florida verteidigten die Demokraten Kathy Castor und Jared Moskowitz ihre Sitze. Die Demokratin Pia Dandiya verteidigte ihren Wahlkreis in Südflorida. Das ist deshalb bemerkenswert, weil die Republikaner die Grenzen aller drei Wahlkreise in diesem Jahr zu ihren Gunsten neu gezogen hatten. Damit wollten sie mehrere bislang demokratisch gehaltene Sitze erobern, um erwartete Verluste in anderen Teilen des Landes auszugleichen.
Bislang haben die Republikaner eine knappe Mehrheit im Repräsentantenhaus - sie halten derzeit noch 218 der 435 Sitze. Bei den Midterms werden alle Sitze im Repräsentantenhaus neu vergeben. 2024 hatte die Republikaner 220 Sitze geholte und die Demokraten 215.
Wichtige Senatsposten für Demokraten
Ob die Demokraten auch in der zweiten Kammer des Kongresses, dem Senat, die Mehrheit erobern können, galt vor der Wahl als fraglicher. Nun deutet vieles auf einen Umschwung hin - in vier Bundesstaaten besiegten Demokraten ihre republikanische Konkurrenz.
In North Carolina verloren die Republikaner laut AP-Berechnungen einen Senatssitz an den Demokraten Roy Cooper. Er setzte sich gegen den Republikaner Michael Whatley durch.
Im benachbarten South Carolina setzte sich laut AP die Demokratin Annie Andrews gegen die Republikanerin Darline Graham Nordone durch. Graham Nordone ist die Schwester des im Sommer gestorbenen republikanischen Senators Lindsey Graham.
In Texas deutet sich eine Überraschung an: Nach AP-Berechnungen wird sich dort der Demokrat James Talarico durchsetzen und so zum ersten Mal seit mehr als 30 Jahren einen Senatssitz für seine Partei dort erobert. Er setzte sich gegen den von Präsident Trump unterstützten Kandidaten Ken Paxton durch.
In Ohio setzte sich der demokratische Kandidat Sherrod Brown durch. Der Sieg markiert für Brown ein Comeback zwei Jahre nach dem Verlust seines Sitzes.
Darüber hinaus gewannen die Demokraten in zehn weiteren Bundesstaaten, die aber als sicher galten. Dazu zählen Delaware, Colorado, Illinois und Massachusetts. Auch in Georgia gewann der Amtsinhaber Jon Ossoff. Die Republikaner verteidigten ihre Senatsposten in Wyoming, Florida, Kentucky und West Virginia.
Es sind zahlreiche Rennen offen, in denen die Republikaner höhere Chancen haben, zu gewinnen. Um die Kontrolle im Senat zu erlangen, müssen die Demokraten insgesamt vier zusätzliche Mandate gewinnen.
Erste schwarze Gouverneurin in den USA?
In 36 Bundesstaaten werden auch Gouverneurinnen und Gouverneure gewählt. In Georgia gewann laut Berechnungen von US-Medien die Demokratin Keisha Lance Bottoms. Die frühere Beraterin von Präsident Joe Biden wäre die erste schwarze Frau der US-Geschichte, die Regierungschefin in einem Bundesstaat wird.
Die Gouverneursämter in von den Republikanern gehaltenen Bundesstaaten Iowa und Texas sind ebenfalls an Demokraten gegangen. Der Rob Sand setzte sich in Iowa gegen den republikanischen Herausforderer Zach Lahn durch, wie aus Daten der Nachrichtenagentur AP hervorgeht. Die Demokratin Gina Hinojosa gewann in Texas gegen Greg Abbott.
Zudem konnten die Demokraten laut Berechnungen in mindestens sieben Bundesstaaten ihre Gouverneursposten verteidigen. Wiedergewählt wurden unter anderem die Gouverneurin von New York, Kathy Hochul, sowie der Gouverneur von Pennsylvania, Josh Shapiro. Die Republikaner verteidigten mindestens zwei Gouverneursposten. In Florida wird laut Prognosen von mindestens zwei Sendern der Republikaner Byron Donalds neuer Gouverneur, er folgt seinem Parteikollegen Ron DeSantis nach.
Gouverneure werden in der Regel für vier Jahre gewählt. Sie haben in ihren Bundestaaten ähnliche Befugnisse wie der US-Präsident für das Land: Sie leiten die Exekutive, können Gesetze billigen oder per Veto verhindern und Richter ernennen.

In Florida wird laut Prognosen von mindestens zwei Sendern der Republikaner Byron Donalds neuer Gouverneur, er folgt seinem Parteikollegen Ron DeSantis nach.
Gouverneure werden in der Regel für vier Jahre gewählt. Sie haben in ihren Bundestaaten ähnliche Befugnisse wie der US-Präsident für das Land: Sie leiten die Exekutive, können Gesetze billigen oder per Veto verhindern und Richter ernennen.

title: Zwischenwahlen in den USA: Warum sind sie wichtig, wer wird gewählt, wo wird's spannend?
content_c:
US-Kongresswahlen: Midterms werden zum Referendum über Trump
3. November 2026
In den USA wird gewählt. Die Amerikanerinnen und Amerikaner stimmen an diesem 3. November aber nicht über den Herrn im Weißen Haus ab, sondern über das Kapitol: Die Midterm elections stehen an.
Diese Zwischenwahlen finden alle vier Jahre statt, immer genau in der zeitlichen Mitte zwischen zwei Präsidentschaftswahlen. Die Wahlberechtigten in den USA entscheiden darüber, wer sie im Repräsentantenhaus und im Senat, den beiden Kongresskammern, vertritt. Außerdem geht es in einigen Bundesstaaten darum, wer Gouverneur oder Gouverneurin werden soll.
Neben diesen Entscheidungen, die klar auf dem Wahlzettel zu sehen sind, wird aber auch noch etwas anderes von den Wählerinnen und Wählern bewertet.
Die Zwischenwahl ist "häufig ein Referendum über den Präsidenten und die Partei, die gerade an der Macht ist", erklärte J. Miles Coleman, Wahlanalyst beim University of Virginia Center for Politics in den USA, vor den letzten Midterms im Jahr 2022. Wenn das Volk zufrieden ist, schneidet die Partei des Mannes im Weißen Haus besser ab, wenn Unzufriedenheit herrscht, schlechter. Aktuell liegen die Zustimmungswerte von Präsident Donald Trump auf einem Rekordtief.
Wen wählen die Amerikaner bei den Midterms?
Alle Sitze im US-Repräsentantenhaus stehen zur Wahl. Wahlberechtigte im ganzen Land stimmen über die 435 Abgeordneten mit Stimmrecht ab. Ein Abgeordneter oder eine Abgeordnete vertritt jeweils einen Wahlkreis. Diese sind auf Basis der Bevölkerungsdichte eingeteilt. So haben verhältnismäßig große Bundesstaaten wie Wyoming, in denen nur wenige Menschen leben, nur einen einzigen Sitz im Repräsentantenhaus. New Jersey, ein flächenmäßig deutlich kleinerer Bundesstaat, in dem aber mehr Menschen leben, hat 12 Sitze. Abgeordnete werden für eine Amtszeit von zwei Jahren gewählt.
Die Amtszeit eines US-Senators dagegen dauert sechs Jahre. Der Senat, die andere Kammer des Kongresses, verfügt über 100 Sitze - zwei für jeden der 50 Bundesstaaten, unabhängig von ihrer Größe. Alle zwei Jahre wird rund ein Drittel der Sitze neu vergeben. Bei den Zwischenwahlen in diesem Jahr stimmen Amerikanerinnen und Amerikaner über 35 Sitze ab. Anders als fürs Repräsentantenhaus wird daher bei den Midterms nicht in jedem Bundesstaat über die Vertretung im Senat abgestimmt.
Außerdem wählen die Menschen in 36 Bundesstaaten ihren Gouverneur oder ihre Gouverneurin. Die Amtszeit liegt meist bei vier Jahren. In den USA werden viele Entscheidungen auf bundesstaatlicher Ebene getroffen, vom Abtreibungsrecht über Bildungsfragen bis hin zur Durchführung aller Wahlen. Ob Demokraten oder Republikaner in einem Staat das Sagen haben, macht somit einen erheblichen Unterschied für das Leben der Bevölkerung.
Wer hat die Mehrheit im US-Kongress?
In beiden Kammern des Kongresses haben aktuell die Republikaner, also die Partei von Präsident Trump, die Mehrheit. Ihr Vorsprung ist allerdings gering.
Im Repräsentantenhaus sitzen derzeit 218 Republikaner, 214 Demokraten und ein unabhängiger Abgeordneter, der normalerweise mit den Republikanern abstimmt. Zwei Sitze sind vakant. Experten sehen es als wahrscheinlich an, dass die Demokraten bei der kommenden Wahl die Mehrheit in dieser Kammer übernehmen. "Es wäre eine Überraschung, wenn die Demokraten nicht mindestens das Repräsentantenhaus gewinnen", sagte Coleman Ende Oktober dem US-TV-Sender CBS.
Im Senat sitzen aktuell 53 Republikaner und 45 Demokraten, sowie zwei unabhängige Senatoren, die normalerweise mit den Demokraten abstimmen. Wenn es bei Abstimmungen im Senat zu einem 50:50-Patt kommt, entscheidet der Vizepräsident. Zurzeit ist somit Trumps Vize, der Republikaner JD Vance, das Zünglein an der Waage.
Warum sind die Zwischenwahlen wichtig?
Die Wahlbeteiligung ist bei den Zwischenwahlen zwar niedriger als bei den Präsidentschaftswahlen, dennoch hat das Ergebnis der Midterms entscheidenden Einfluss auf die US-Politik der kommenden Jahre. Während der US-Präsident viel Macht hat und einiges per Erlass (den berüchtigten "executive orders") entscheiden kann, müssen viele Maßnahmen vom Kongress genehmigt werden, sonst können sie nicht umgesetzt werden.
Für Trump ist es also wesentlich einfacher, die USA in seinem Sinne zu führen, wenn die Republikaner in beiden Kongresskammern die Mehrheit haben. Sollten die Demokraten in einer oder sogar beiden Kammern die Mehrheit gewinnen, würde es für Trump schwieriger werden, innen- und außenpolitische Änderungen durchzusetzen.
Wo sind die entscheidenden Rennen?
Im US-Repräsentantenhaus müssten die Demokraten insgesamt nur vier Sitze hinzugewinnen, um mit 218 Abgeordneten die Mehrheit zu übernehmen. Von den 435 Entscheidungen gelten nur wenige als völlig offen. Zu ihnen gehören unter anderem Distrikte in Iowa, Virginia und Montana.
Bei den Senatswahlen ist beispielsweise das Rennen in Texas spannend. In aktuellen Umfragen liegt der Demokrat James Talarico gleichauf mit seinem republikanischen Rivalen Ken Paxton. Für eine Mehrheit im US-Senat müssten die Demokraten ebenfalls vier Sitze hinzugewinnen, was als ungleich schwieriger gilt. Aber dass Texas einer davon sein könnte, ist eine Sensation. Seit 1994 hat kein Demokrat hier auf bundesstaatlicher Ebene gewinnen können. Talarico wird sogar von einigen Mitgliedern der Bush-Familie unterstützt, der republikanischen Dynastie, aus der die Präsidenten George H. W. Bush und sein Sohn, George W. Bush, hervorgingen.
Dieser aktualisierte und gekürzte Artikel wurde erstmals am 27. Oktober veröffentlicht.
description: Die US-Amerikaner wählen ihren neuen Kongress: Senat, Abgeordnetenhaus, Gouverneure - die Zwischenwahlen stellen wichtige Weichen für die Zukunft der USA. Und sie bewerten immer auch die Politik des Präsidenten.

title: Зрання Росія атакує Україну реактивними дронами: де стались вибухи і є загроза (мапа)
content_c:
Зрання Росія атакує Україну реактивними дронами: де стались вибухи і є загроза (мапа)
Українців закликають не ігнорувати сигнали повітряної тривоги та перебувати в укриттях.
Вранці 4 листопада російська армія продовжує атакувати Україну безпілотниками. Повітряні Сили ЗСУ повідомляють про рух ворожих цілей одразу в кількох областях.
Що відомо про російську атаку на Україну — читайте у матеріалі ТСН.ua.
Станом на 07:20 у низці областей оголошено «жовту» тривогу. Зокрема, у Черкаській області дрони помітили поблизу Тального, у Кіровоградській — біля Благовіщенського. На Полтавщині ударні БпЛА зафіксували в районі Решетилівки та Глобиного, а також у напрямку Миргорода.
Крім того, реактивні дрони летіли північніше Павлограда та в районі Березанки на Миколаївщині. Ще один реактивний БпЛА зайшов із Брянської області РФ на північ Чернігівщини.
Де лунали вибухи
На світанку сирени лунали у регіонах на заході. Після 4 ранку серія вибухів пролунала у місті Рівне. У Повітряних силах ЗСУ інформували про рух дронів у напрямку міста.
Гучно було і в Тернопілі та районі. Внаслідок російської атаки сталось влучання БпЛА.

title: БПЛА атаковали логистический центр Ozon в Адыгейске: вспыхнул пожар
content_c:
В ночь на 4 ноября беспилотники атаковали логистический центр компании Ozon в Адыгейске. ASTRA со ссылкой на компанию сообщает, что всех сотрудников эвакуировали. Также на месте удара вспыхнул пожар.
В пресс-службе Ozon отметили, что товары из поврежденного комплекса временно уберут с сайта маркетплейса. Заказы, которые не удастся доставить с других складов, отменят. Также там прекратили принимать товары от продавцов, а грузы, которые уже направляются в центр, перенаправляют на другие склады.
В то же время, по их словам, покупатели могут и дальше оформлять заказы — их будут собирать в других логистических центрах и доставлять по обычной схеме.
О масштабах разрушений в компании не сообщили.
Российские маркетплейсы Wildberries и Ozon, понесшие миллиардные убытки из-за ударов украинских беспилотников, столкнулись с новой проблемой — продавцы массово подают против них иски. Так, с 15 июля по 15 сентября против ООО «РВБ», владеющего Wildberries, подали 599 исков. Это на 53% больше, чем за аналогичный период прошлого года. Компания «Интернет Решения», управляющая Ozon, за это время получила 236 новых исков — что более чем вдвое больше, чем в 2025 году. Чаще всего иски против маркетплейсов подают небольшие компании, продающие товары через интернет.
Начиная с июля Украина нанесла более 30 ударов по логистическим центрам, которыми пользуются крупнейшие российские онлайн-магазины Wildberries и Ozon. В результате атак на некоторых складах возникли сильные пожары, что поставило под угрозу работу тысяч сторонних продавцов, реализующих товары через эти популярные платформы.
Экономист Алексей Пластун в статье «Российская экономика вступает в системный кризис. Насколько близка «игла Кощея»» объясняет, почему обнуление лидера e-commerce за месяц — не случайность, а симптом, и что произойдет, когда та же логика дойдет до Ozon и всей банковской системы.

title: "Ми поїхали у відпустку з сусідами - і після цього помінялися родинами"
content_c:
"Ми поїхали у відпустку з сусідами - і після цього помінялися родинами"
  - Author, Емілі Дауті
  - Role, ВВС
- Published
- Час прочитання: 5 хв
Рейчел Стоун з Британії було п'ять років, а її братові Ієну - 10, коли батьки взяли їх на відпочинок у кемпінгу в Уельсі разом із родиною, яка жила по сусідству.
Вони провели разом два сповнені веселощів тижні. Але коли повернулися додому, кожна сім'я розділилася навпіл, і вони помінялися будинками.
Рейчел і її мати Кей переїхали до сусіда Едді та його доньки Елісон. Дружина Едді, Ірен, та їхня донька Дон переїхали до батька Рейчел, Рекса, та її брата Ієна.
Рейчел розповіла ведучій подкасту Radio 4 Life Changing докторці Шіан Вільямс про травму від розпаду родини, хаос, який після цього настав, і про те, як їй зрештою вдалося пробачити батьків.
Спочатку Рейчел та Ієн були в захваті, коли у будинку по сусідству на острові Шеппі в Англії, де вони мешкали, оселилася нова родина.
"Ми всі четверо одразу знайшли спільну мову", - каже вона.
Вони страшенно раділи майбутній спільній відпустці.
Рейчел згадує два будинки на колесах, припарковані поруч, і поїздку на гору Сноудон.
Але коли настав час повертатися додому, усе переплуталося - люди сідали не в ті автомобілі.
Рейчел пам'ятає, як мати, сидячи на передньому пасажирському сидінні, обернулася до неї й сказала: "У нас тепер буде нова сім'я. Ми житимемо в будинку номер вісім з Едді та Елісон. Елісон стане твоєю новою сестрою".
"А твій тато й брат і далі житимуть у будинку номер десять. Там житимуть тітка Ірен і Дон. А Дон стане новою сестрою твого брата", - додала вона.
Рейчел одразу відчула "сильну тривогу, страх і розгубленість" і, за її словами, почала плакати.
Поки автомобіль гуркотів дорогою, вона почувалася "збентеженою, але водночас трохи схвильованою". Елісон їй подобалася, і вона завжди хотіла мати сестру.
Того вечора Елісон дозволила їй спати на верхньому ярусі двоярусного ліжка, а наступного ранку дорослі перевезли речі з одного будинку до іншого.
Рейчел каже, що почувалася дуже розгубленою.
"Не можеш не думати, що це твоя провина", - каже вона.
Життя в будинку номер вісім, де тепер мешкала Рейчел, дуже відрізнялося від того, до якого вона звикла в будинку номер десять. Її колишній дім був чистим, а в новому було "собача шерсть, жирні речі, автомобільний мотлох".
Мати вона описує як "вимогливу, але справедливу" й дуже практичну жінку.
Вітчим Едді "ніколи не був зі мною жорстоким, але я ніколи не називала його татом. Я не була його дівчинкою".
Їй також дуже бракувало Ієна.
"Я ним дуже пишалася. Він був моїм старшим братом. Коли я була зовсім маленькою, то чекала в палісаднику, поки він повернеться зі школи", - згадує Рейчел.
Рейчел було сім років, коли обидві пари разом звернулися до суду й розлучилися. Згодом вони одружилися зі своїми новими партнерами на окремих скромних церемоніях.
Рейчел навіть не знала, що її батько одружився з Ірен, аж поки не побачила весільну фотографію. Приблизно у 11-12 років вона почала дедалі рідше навідуватися до свого колишнього дому. За її словами, їй було важко їздити до батька, а з Ірен вона не ладнала.
Тим часом життя з матір'ю Кей та Едді було хаотичним.
"[Він] був доволі владним і схильним усе контролювати. Коли мені виповнилося 13, мама сказала: "Так далі тривати не може, ми не можемо так жити", - згадує Рейчел.
Вона каже, що школа була для неї "способом утекти". Вона добре вчилася й стала вчителькою.
Згодом Рейчел вийшла заміж і народила двох синів, але тепер розлучена з чоловіком і працює бізнес-коучем.
Упродовж усього життя мати Рейчел відмовлялася говорити про обмін сім'ями. "Я ставила багато запитань. Вона відповідала, що все складно".
Через десятиліття, під час сімейної відпустки зі своїми синами, Рейчел знову повернулася до цієї теми.
"Я сказала мамі: "О, Джозефу вже десять... Ієну було десять, коли ти дозволила йому поїхати з татом та Ірен".
За словами Рейчел, її мати була "сама не своя від почуття провини й сорому... через власні егоїстичні рішення".
"Через багато років вона нарешті сказала мені ті слова, які я, мабуть, усе життя хотіла почути: "Мені дуже шкода, що я тебе підвела. Я хочу спробувати все виправити".
Рейчел каже, що саме тоді почалося відновлення її "чудових" стосунків із матір'ю.
Рейчел ніколи не мала близьких стосунків із батьком.
"Він сказав мені, що мав вибір між дружиною та дітьми. На жаль для мене, він обрав дружину", - каже вона.
Він та Ірен залишалися разом до його смерті у віці 81 року.
Але коли Рейчел виступала на похороні батька, вона сказала, що відчувала, ніби має попросити в нього вибачення.
"Я вигадала образ ідеального батька, якого в мене відібрали... Я створила в уяві надлюдину, яка могла б бути для мене всім. І я хотіла, щоб він був саме таким. Але водночас вважаю, що треба приймати людей такими, якими вони є", - каже Рейчел.
"Думаю, батьки роблять усе, що можуть... Не можна вимагати від них бути кимось іншим", - додає вона.

title: Демократи здобувають ключові перемоги на проміжних виборах до Конгресу США під час підрахунку голосів – ЗМІ
content_c:
Представники Демократичної партії здобувають низку важливих перемог у ключових штатах на проміжних виборах до Сенату та Палати представників Конгресу США, які визначать подальший баланс сил у Вашингтоні, повідомляють агентство The Associated Press та видання The Guardian у середу вранці за підсумками закриття виборчих дільниць у більшості американських штатів.
Загалом під час голосування 3 листопада американські виборці переобирають усі 435 місць у Палаті представників та 35 зі 100 крісел у Сенаті США, де до виборів республіканці утримували більшість у співвідношенні 53 на 47 мандатів.
За оприлюдненими прогнозами на виборах до верхньої палати Конгресу, колишній губернатор Північної Кароліни демократ Рой Купер виборов вакантне місце у Сенаті, ставши першим за 10 років представником Демократичної партії від цього штату у верхній палаті. Крім того, чинні сенатори-демократи Джон Оссофф у Джорджії та Марк Ворнер у Вірджинії успішно переобралися на новий термін, здолавши республіканців Майка Коллінза і Берта Мізусаву відповідно. У Нью-Гемпширі конгресмен-демократ Кріс Паппас зберіг за своєю партією сенатське крісло у протистоянні з екссенатором-республіканцем Джоном Сунуну, тоді як у Флориді представниця Республіканської партії Ешлі Муді перемогла демократку Енджі Ніксон на позачергових виборах до Сенату.
На виборах до Палати представників демократи захистили низку округів у Флориді з переглянутими межами, де перемогу здобули конгресмени Джаред Московіц, Кеті Кастор і Деббі Вассерман-Шульц, а демократка Ребекка Беннетт відібрала у республіканців округ у штаті Нью-Джерсі.
Одночасно на губернаторських виборах, які проходять у 26 штатах паралельно з сенатськими перегонами, республіканець Байрон Дональдс переміг у боротьбі за посаду губернатора Флориди, а демократка Кіша Ленс Боттомс здобула перемогу на виборах губернатора Джорджії. Також свої посади зберегли чинні губернатори-демократи Джей Бі Пріцкер в Іллінойсі та Джош Шапіро у Пенсильванії. За даними екзитполів, головними темами для виборців під час волевиявлення стали стан економіки та захист демократії.
Як повідомлялося, у вівторок американці вирушать на виборчі дільниці, щоб проголосувати на проміжних виборах до Конгресу США.

title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
content_c:
Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
- Published
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".
It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
North Korea involvement
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."
As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

title: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
content_c:
King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
- Published
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.
There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.
While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.
He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."
He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."
King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."
The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.
The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.
"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.
"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.
"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."
The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

title: Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
content_c:
Asda hires ex-Morrisons boss in bid to grow firm
- Published
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.
Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.
Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.
Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.
"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.
Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.
According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.
"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.
"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."
Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.
But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

title: Alleged attack on One Nation supporter not believed to be politically motivated, Victoria police say
content_c:
An alleged attack on a One Nation supporter is not believed to have been politically motivated, Victoria police say, clarifying that a “blunt weapon” was allegedly used rather than a baseball bat as originally reported.
On Tuesday, police confirmed they arrested a 37-year-old Hampton Park man and a 14-year-old boy over the alleged attack on a 60-year-old man outside his Torquay home on Sunday night.
“It is believed they allegedly assaulted the man with a baseball bat before being arrested by attending units a short time later,” police said on Tuesday.
But on Wednesday, police had removed references to the baseball bat from their statement and instead alleged a “blunt weapon” was used.
“Detectives are not treating the incident as politically motivated,” a spokesperson said.
Police are believed to be treating the incident as a random attack.
Prior to the alleged attack on Sunday, police intercepted a vehicle on Blackgate Road – a few kilometres from the victim’s Torquay home. The driver, a 37-year-old man from Hampton Park, allegedly returned a positive breath test and his vehicle was impounded. He is expected to be charged on summons.
Police said the man smashed the windows of his own vehicle during the incident.
The Hampton Park man was charged with intentionally causing injury and other assault-related offences, and was remanded in custody to appear again on 10 November, while the boy was issued with a caution.
Leaders from across the political spectrum condemned the alleged attack, with One Nation’s federal leader, Pauline Hanson, visiting the alleged victim in Geelong hospital on Tuesday and the party launching an online fundraiser, which was later shared on X by Elon Musk. As of 1pm Wednesday, it had raised more than $250,000.
One Nation said on Wednesday it would not comment.
On Tuesday, Hanson alleged the victim had been “kicked [so] badly he lost consciousness”. He was left “bleeding from basically every orifice in his face”, as well as bleeding in the brain, she told reporters outside the hospital on Tuesday.
“It was a vicious attack. It wasn’t just a punch,” Hanson alleged. “Even now, with the bleed, it still could be life-threatening.”
The party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said on Tuesday the victim was a volunteer and alleged the incident began when the man and the boy “interfered with” the One Nation signs on his property.
“Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country,” Pickering said.
“If you don’t like someone’s politics, you vote accordingly. You don’t [allegedly] assault them.”
Speaking on ABC Radio Melbourne on Wednesday morning, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll reiterated his condemnation of the alleged attack, describing it as “abhorrent” and “disgusting”.
“This man putting up corflutes is entitled to do that. Every Victorian, no matter whether they’re wearing an orange, blue, red – or green for that matter – T-shirt, is entitled to put their case forward in a civil matter, in a civil way,” Carroll said.

title: Burnham denies proposing return to free movement in talks with EU
content_c:
Andy Burnham has denied proposing a return of free movement in talks between the UK and EU, saying any decision about the future relationship will be led by the will of the British people.
His comments came as two senior ministers expressed caution about the talk of the UK returning as a full member of the EU or single market and the consequences of a return to free movement.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said on Monday she wanted to abide by Labour’s manifesto, which ruled out free movement.
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said he wanted an “honest discussion” about how leaving the EU had affected migration, saying it was replacing temporary migrants from Europe with those from elsewhere who had more dependents and settled for longer.
“I have not proposed freedom of movement coming back,” he said. “I do believe that we should have an honest discussion with people about how immigration has changed since the Brexit vote because the shorter-term migration of people coming from Europe and then going back has been replaced with long-term settlement in bigger numbers, and that was the Boriswave.”
The prime minister said the EU summit in November would cement a deal on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, and discussions would then move on to how the UK could secure a long-term stable deal with the EU, with all options on the table.
A draft text has been circulated among the 27 EU members, suggesting a final deal is close. The Guardian reported that UK ministers were prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees if Brussels allowed the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
Burnham told ITV that he believed public opinion had shifted on EU membership but he would “not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”
He said for this parliament he was committed to the red lines in Labour’s manifesto, ruling out a return to the customs union, single market or free movement.
Mahmood, who introduced sweeping changes to migration rules in parliament on Monday, said she would not indulge the speculation about freedom of movement.
“What I am keen on is abiding by our manifesto,” she told Sky News. “The prime minister has himself recognised that there were significant issues with the free movement of people, and that should also be part of the debate that we’re going to have as a country about our Brexit settlement and what we do for the future.”
But she said there had been a loss of control over migration post-Brexit and said losing access to EU-wide databases had “had a very significant impact on us and our ability to manage migration into this country”.
Asked if she had been consulted about the prime minister’s comments, she said she had discussed the issue with Burnham.
“I think the prime minister said that he wants to have an open discussion,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “I think he’s got a position that actually most of the country can understand, which is we’re 10 years on from Brexit, it’s right that we have an open discussion about the terms on which we left and what the right thing is for our future.
“It’s also been really clear that we are absolutely bound by the terms of our manifesto. We had a manifesto commitment not to reopen in this parliament the question of freedom of movement, and that will not change in this parliament.”
The immigration minister, Anna Turley, told Sky she wanted to prioritise getting more young British people into jobs. “My priority is sorting out the system that we’ve got, getting young people in my constituency into work, making sure we’ve got an immigration system that is not chaotic, that is controlled, that we stop the illegal migration through small boats, that we get a grip on removals,” she said.

He said for this parliament he was committed to the red lines in Labour’s manifesto, ruling out a return to the customs union, single market or free movement.
Mahmood, who introduced sweeping changes to migration rules in parliament on Monday, said she would not indulge the speculation about freedom of movement.
“What I am keen on is abiding by our manifesto,” she told Sky News. “The prime minister has himself recognised that there were significant issues with the free movement of people, and that should also be part of the debate that we’re going to have as a country about our Brexit settlement and what we do for the future.”
But she said there had been a loss of control over migration post-Brexit and said losing access to EU-wide databases had “had a very significant impact on us and our ability to manage migration into this country”.
Asked if she had been consulted about the prime minister’s comments, she said she had discussed the issue with Burnham.
“I think the prime minister said that he wants to have an open discussion,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “I think he’s got a position that actually most of the country can understand, which is we’re 10 years on from Brexit, it’s right that we have an open discussion about the terms on which we left and what the right thing is for our future.
“It’s also been really clear that we are absolutely bound by the terms of our manifesto. We had a manifesto commitment not to reopen in this parliament the question of freedom of movement, and that will not change in this parliament.”
The immigration minister, Anna Turley, told Sky she wanted to prioritise getting more young British people into jobs. “My priority is sorting out the system that we’ve got, getting young people in my constituency into work, making sure we’ve got an immigration system that is not chaotic, that is controlled, that we stop the illegal migration through small boats, that we get a grip on removals,” she said.

title: Greenland's parliament ratifies Trump's US security agreement
content_c:
Greenland's parliament ratifies Trump's US security agreement
November 3, 2026
Greenland's parliament on Tuesday signed off on a trilateral security and military-access agreement with the United States and Denmark that paves the way for an expanded US' military presence on the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
The deal has alleviated pressure coming from US President Donald Trump, who earlier this year had repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory, citing US security interests.
After months of negotiation the agreement was signed in September by Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
The agreement allows for two new US military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system. It also keeps Greenland under Danish control, while reaffirming Greenlanders' right to self determination.
Greenland cannot take 'stability for granted'
On Tuesday, shortly before the vote in the capital, Nuuk, Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede welcomed the agreement's ratification.
"We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted," Egede said.
In a first debate last month, a majority of Greenlandic lawmakers had already signalled support for the agreement.
Pele Broberg, chair of the pro-independence Naleraq party, questioned the deal's value for Greenland.
"We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement," Broberg said.
The agreement will come into effect after ratification by the Danish parliament, which is due to read the bill over two sessions in November. A vote is scheduled for November 19 in Copenhagen.
Trump pressures Greenland
In January 2026, Trump began calling for the US to control Greenland, and threatened the use of military force and tariffs against US European allies if he did not get his way.
Trump had claimed that Denmark was not doing enough to defend its autonomous arctic territory from unspecified threats from China and Russia.
Trump's repeated threats damaged US ties with Denmark and rattled the US' European NATO allies.
On January 21, after Trump met with NATO chief Mark Rutte on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, tensions cooled after Rutte and Trump announced a "concept of a deal" allowing for expanded US defense access to Greenland, which would later evolve into the agreement signed in September.
Denmark had repeatedly said it was willing to discuss expanding the US military footprint in Greenland, while rejecting Trump's more extreme demand that Greenland become US territory.
Critics have pointed out the same deal could have been made without the extreme disruption caused by Trump's territorial and tariff threats.
Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has considerable military freedom of action in Greenland.
After years of voluntarily drawing down its military presence, the US only maintains the Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which is used for missile defense and radar surveillance.
description: The US is set to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island, part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It follows pressure from Donald Trump earlier in the year which opened a major rift in the transatlantic alliance.

title: News: Midterms in den USA, Rechter NSU-Terror, Brückentage 2027
content_c:
Die Lage am Morgen Die Quittung für Trump
- Die USA haben gewählt – der Verlierer heißt Donald Trump.
- Vor 15 Jahren flog der NSU auf – doch rechten Terror gibt es immer noch.
- Haben Sie ihren Urlaub für 2027 schon geplant? Mit Brückentagen können Sie mehr herausholen.
Die US-Amerikaner haben entschieden
Eine blaue Welle schwappt durch die USA. Schon kurz nach Schließung der Wahllokale zeigte sich: Die Demokraten werden die Zwischenwahlen mit deutlichem Vorsprung gewinnen. Ihre blaue Farbe dominierte die Wahlkarten.
Die US-Wählerinnen und -Wähler haben über die Besetzung des Repräsentantenhauses und offene Sitze im Senat abgestimmt. In beiden Kammern hatten Donald Trumps Republikaner bislang die Mehrheit. Damit ist nun offenbar Schluss. Die Auszählung läuft zwar noch, doch mehreren US-Medien zufolge ist der Vorsprung der Demokraten im Senat und im Repräsentantenhaus nicht mehr einzuholen.
Großbildschirm mit CNN-Prognosen in Atlanta
Foto: Bloomberg / Getty Images
US-Präsident Donald Trump kündigte an, die Ergebnisse der Kongresswahlen zu akzeptieren. »Wir werden mit den Demokraten zusammenarbeiten, und wir freuen uns schon darauf«, sagte er der »New York Times«. Man werde »wahrscheinlich« eine Lösung finden. Eine persönliche Verantwortung für das Wahlergebnis wies er auf Truth Social von sich: »Ich stand nicht auf dem Stimmzettel.«
- Alle Entwicklungen rund um die Midterms hier in der Liveanalyse
Der rechte Terror lebt
Heute vor 15 Jahren gegen Mittag brannte in einer Nebenstraße in Eisenach ein Wohnmobil, darin fand die Polizei die Leichen von zwei Rechtsterroristen. Ich nenne ihre Namen hier nicht, sie sind eines Gedenkens nicht würdig.
Ausgebranntes Wohnmobil der NSU-Terroristen, 4. November 2011
Foto: SPIEGEL ONLINE
Erinnern müssen wir uns aber an ihre Taten: Als Terrorgruppe »Nationalsozialistischer Untergrund« (NSU) ermordeten sie zwischen 2000 und 2007 neun Migranten und eine Polizistin, begingen 43 Mordversuche, drei Sprengstoffanschläge und 15 Raubüberfälle. Unterstützt wurden sie dabei von zahlreichen, wechselnden Helfern aus dem rechtsextremen Milieu.
Und obwohl die beiden Männer und ihre später festgenommene Mittäterin den Behörden über viele Jahre als gefährliche Rechtsextreme bekannt waren, wurden sie zu Lebzeiten nie mit den Morden an den Migranten und der Polizistin in Verbindung gebracht.
Die Ermittler, die Medien und die Öffentlichkeit glaubten lieber daran, dass die Mordopfer in irgendwelche mafiösen Strukturen verstrickt und womöglich selbst kriminell gewesen seien. Dass die Ermordeten vollkommen unbescholten und die Täter deutsche Neonazis waren, das konnte man sich nicht vorstellen (mehr dazu hier ).
Heute vor 15 Jahren nahmen sich die beiden NSU-Terroristen das Leben, aber die Gefahr durch Rechtsextreme für unser Land ist geblieben, wenn nicht sogar größer geworden. Der Kern des NSU bestand aus nur drei Untergetauchten.
Ende September 2025, das ist der aktuell verfügbare Stand, waren 515 Personen auf freiem Fuß, gegen die Haftbefehle wegen rechtsextremer Straftaten vorlagen. Und erst am Freitag hat die Polizei einen jungen Mann in Niedersachsen festgenommen, der mit einem gefüllten Benzinkanister unterwegs war und geplant haben soll, eine Flüchtlingsunterkunft anzuzünden. Der Anschlag soll in einer rechtsextremen Chatgruppe namens »Terror 18« geplant worden sein. Der Verdächtige ist erst 15 Jahre alt.
- Mehr Hintergründe hier: Teenager mit gefülltem Benzinkanister gestoppt
Mehr Urlaub geht nicht
Wenn Sie zu den ganz besonders Schlauen gehören, dann haben Sie das selbstverständlich alles schon selbst recherchiert und den gesamten Jahresurlaub für das kommende Jahr bereits durchoptimiert, geplant und auch schon eingereicht. Falls Sie aber ein wenig so sind wie ich, also etwas langsamer, dann sind es Neuigkeiten, die mein Kollege Bastian Midasch zusammengestellt hat.
Blick auf Polignano a Mare, Italien
Foto: Handout/ Getty Images
Und zwar leider keine besonders freizeitförderlichen: 2027 fallen nur etwa die Hälfte der bundesweiten gesetzlichen Feiertage auf Wochentage (mehr hier ). Aber wenn Sie die Brückentage geschickt nutzen, können Sie dennoch etwas mehr aus dem Urlaub herausholen. Also gesetzt den Fall, die lieben Brückentagsspezialisten unter Ihren Kollegen haben da noch etwas für Sie freigelassen im Dienstplan.
Aber haben Arbeitnehmer überhaupt Anspruch auf freie Brückentage? Kann der Chef Betriebsurlaub an Brückentagen sogar anordnen? Und wie ist es, wenn alle aus dem Team am Brückentag freinehmen wollen? Bastian hat dazu mit dem Hamburger Arbeitsrechtler Daniel Brügger gesprochen. Mein Rat: Zuerst lesen Sie dessen Antworten auf SPIEGEL.de. Und dann füllen Sie fix Ihren Urlaubsantrag aus.
- Mehr Hintergründe hier: Habe ich einen Anspruch auf freie Brückentage?
Hier geht’s zum aktuellen Tagesquiz
Noch mehr Rätsel wie Viererkette, Wordle und Paarsuche finden Sie bei SPIEGEL Games.
Verlierer des Tages …
Zugspitze im Schnee
Foto: IMAGO / ingimage
… ist ein 21-Jähriger aus Bayern, der mitten in der Nacht am frühen 1. November seine 17-jährige Begleiterin bei minus zwölf Grad an der Zugspitze auf rund 2500 Meter Höhe zurückgelassen hat und ohne sie abgestiegen ist. Zum Glück konnte die Frau gerettet werden. Gegen den Mann ermittelt jetzt die Polizei.
- Die ganze Geschichte hier: Der Mann steigt ab, die Frau bleibt allein in der Gipfelwand zurück – bei minus zwölf Grad
Die jüngsten Meldungen aus der Nacht
- Verband fordert 500 Euro Bußgeld für Handy am Steuer: Während der Fahrt das Smartphone in die Hand nehmen – das kann zu schweren Unfällen führen. Verkehrsminister Steffen Bilger macht sich für Handyblitzer stark. Der Verkehrssicherheitsrat hat noch eine andere Idee.
- Google blockiert Suchfunktion, wenn Schulen KI ablehnen: Der großflächige Einsatz von künstlicher Intelligenz an US-Schulen stößt bei Lehrern und Eltern zunehmend auf Widerstand. Google reagiert darauf mit strikten neuen Nutzungsregeln.
- Formel-1-Pilot Ocon fliegt raus – junger Brasilianer übernimmt: In Mexiko wurde er kurzfristig aus dem Cockpit verbannt, jetzt ist für Esteban Ocon endgültig Schluss: Er verliert seinen Platz im Team Haas. Die Hintergründe bleiben nebulös.
Heute bei SPIEGEL Extra: Knapp 3400 Euro Eigenanteil fürs Heim – was mit Ihrem Ersparten passiert
Anna Tolipova / AnnaStills / picture alliance
Die Pflege im Heim wird für immer mehr Menschen unbezahlbar. Expertin Silke Möhring erklärt, wann die Kinder einspringen müssen und ob es sich überhaupt noch lohnt, Geld zurückzulegen .
Ich wünsche Ihnen einen guten Start in den Tag.
Ihr Stefan Kuzmany, Autor der Chefredaktion
