title: British people don’t need to apologise for slavery – but the government does | Olivette Otele
content_c:
Departing from his predecessors’ stances, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, surprised us all when he stated he was open to listening to calls for an apology for the UK’s role in centuries of transatlantic enslavement. King Charles is expected to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” about the UK’s role in the transatlantic slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda today. Burnham was quick to add that financial reparations were off the table. But he was in favour of discussions about debt restructuring – one of the key concerns of the Caribbean community (Caricom) and the African Union. The opposition, led by Kemi Badenoch, argued that apologies were a distraction.
Beyond political bickering and point-scoring lies a deeper question. Why does Britain struggle to fully understand its colonial past and to grapple with the negative impact of its legacies? One the one hand, the country celebrates its historical conquests as far back as the Battle of Hastings and applauds the wealth that derived from the products of colonisation, such as cotton. On the other, it refuses to accept that harm was caused to populations whose lands it forcefully occupied – and that the trafficking of African captives has changed how we think and what we assume about different racial groups to this day.
The king and the PM clearly understand that Caribbean countries, and the Commonwealth as a whole, are among Britain’s most important relationships. The group of 56 Commonwealth countries represents about a third of the world’s population with more than 2.7 billion people. Because of their historical links to Britain, these countries play an important role in the UK’s global influence and soft power. Refusing to apologise and work together towards a reparatory justice plan is a diplomatic and political mistake. In the long run, it also has a knock-on effect on trading partnerships, as Burnham seems to acknowledge.
The question of repair continues to be framed along the lines of financial compensation. That framing fails to consider how the past is weighing on the present and future of British citizens. Repairing includes building a society that is honest about its traumas and ready to work towards reconciliation. In these times of recession, drawing on existing resources could help address points raised by Caricom and the African Union. For example, the return of cultural heritage could be facilitated by having a discussion in parliament about the British Museum Act 1963 and the National Heritage Act 1983, which prevent the British Museum, Natural History Museum, V&A and Science Museum from permanently returning certain objects from their collections.
A fair reparatory justice plan would help tackle issues such as education, climate justice, health inequality and so on. Perhaps the PM has been paying attention to Caricom’s focus on green energy and climate resilience. His pledge of £40m to Caribbean projects is a very significant step towards mending fences and furthering dialogue on climate justice. Education could also be an important part of the plan precisely because part of the British public doesn’t understand why apologies are required, let alone why taxpayers should pay the bill for financial reparations at a time of national and even global economic recession. Lack of knowledge – of how the trafficking of African captives for more than 300 years helped shape British institutions such as parliament, the Church of England, universities, the banking system, royal societies and so on – has led many to wonder why they should apologise for their ancestors.
Transatlantic enslavement centuries ago relied on the labour of enslaved Africans, and it made Britain very wealthy. The institution of slavery classified populations based on a racist hierarchy. It developed the so-called scientific racism of the 19th century, which led to the 21st-century eugenicists’ stances that still influence current debate about belonging and identity.
Tracie Jolliff, an organisational development consultant who specialises in dismantling systemic racism, puts it like this: “There appears to be a collective amnesia when it comes to harms towards people with black skins as compared to other atrocities that have been well documented. Racism still shapes the way the descendants of those same African people are treated today.”
For Jolliff, the ideas that informed and perpetuated transatlantic enslavement never went away; they simply morphed into more subtle, but still life-limiting structural racism. The evidence and outcomes of that can be seen in the ways that British citizens who are black are disadvantaged in housing, health, education and the criminal justice system. Similarly, Marvin Rees, a former mayor of Bristol who is involved with the Repair Campaign, says, “Individuals today are not responsible for their ancestors’ wrongdoings. It is, however, important to make a link between individuals and institutions. Individuals inherited institutions and institutions bestowed advantages.”
Arguments that position reparations as a subject of the distant past are overlooking the facts. UK taxpayers have been paying back the colossal sum that compensated the owners of enslaved people after the Abolition Act 1833 – a bill that was only repaid in full in 2015. It’s not British people who should apologise, but the British government that used taxpayers’ money to compensate those who profited from trading in people.
Because of the legacies of this trade, many descendants of those responsible for transatlantic enslavement are still part of the financial elite of this world. Some of them, like the Heirs of Slavery, are attempting to engage with the question. The UK government should work with families whose ancestors received compensation in 1837 and who are ready to work towards a restorative justice plan – and with institutions such as the Church of England, Lloyd’s of London and universities that have started to do the work. Combining resources is the way forward now.
Black communities who have their life chances negatively affected by systemic racism were also paying the bill for the owners of their ancestors until 2015. So, if the debt to the slavers can endure without question into this century, surely repair for the legacies of ongoing systemic injustices should be dealt with on similar terms.
- 
  Olivette Otele is a historian and distinguished research professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London

content:
Departing from his predecessors’ stances, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, surprised us all when he stated he was open to listening to calls for an apology for the UK’s role in centuries of transatlantic enslavement. King Charles is expected to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” about the UK’s role in the transatlantic slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda today. Burnham was quick to add that financial reparations were off the table. But he was in favour of discussions about debt restructuring – one of the key concerns of the Caribbean community (Caricom) and the African Union. The opposition, led by Kemi Badenoch, argued that apologies were a distraction.
Beyond political bickering and point-scoring lies a deeper question. Why does Britain struggle to fully understand its colonial past and to grapple with the negative impact of its legacies? One the one hand, the country celebrates its historical conquests as far back as the Battle of Hastings and applauds the wealth that derived from the products of colonisation, such as cotton. On the other, it refuses to accept that harm was caused to populations whose lands it forcefully occupied – and that the trafficking of African captives has changed how we think and what we assume about different racial groups to this day.
The king and the PM clearly understand that Caribbean countries, and the Commonwealth as a whole, are among Britain’s most important relationships. The group of 56 Commonwealth countries represents about a third of the world’s population with more than 2.7 billion people. Because of their historical links to Britain, these countries play an important role in the UK’s global influence and soft power. Refusing to apologise and work together towards a reparatory justice plan is a diplomatic and political mistake. In the long run, it also has a knock-on effect on trading partnerships, as Burnham seems to acknowledge.
The question of repair continues to be framed along the lines of financial compensation. That framing fails to consider how the past is weighing on the present and future of British citizens. Repairing includes building a society that is honest about its traumas and ready to work towards reconciliation. In these times of recession, drawing on existing resources could help address points raised by Caricom and the African Union. For example, the return of cultural heritage could be facilitated by having a discussion in parliament about the British Museum Act 1963 and the National Heritage Act 1983, which prevent the British Museum, Natural History Museum, V&A and Science Museum from permanently returning certain objects from their collections.
A fair reparatory justice plan would help tackle issues such as education, climate justice, health inequality and so on. Perhaps the PM has been paying attention to Caricom’s focus on green energy and climate resilience. His pledge of £40m to Caribbean projects is a very significant step towards mending fences and furthering dialogue on climate justice. Education could also be an important part of the plan precisely because part of the British public doesn’t understand why apologies are required, let alone why taxpayers should pay the bill for financial reparations at a time of national and even global economic recession. Lack of knowledge – of how the trafficking of African captives for more than 300 years helped shape British institutions such as parliament, the Church of England, universities, the banking system, royal societies and so on – has led many to wonder why they should apologise for their ancestors.
Transatlantic enslavement centuries ago relied on the labour of enslaved Africans, and it made Britain very wealthy. The institution of slavery classified populations based on a racist hierarchy. It developed the so-called scientific racism of the 19th century, which led to the 21st-century eugenicists’ stances that still influence current debate about belonging and identity.
Tracie Jolliff, an organisational development consultant who specialises in dismantling systemic racism, puts it like this: “There appears to be a collective amnesia when it comes to harms towards people with black skins as compared to other atrocities that have been well documented. Racism still shapes the way the descendants of those same African people are treated today.”
For Jolliff, the ideas that informed and perpetuated transatlantic enslavement never went away; they simply morphed into more subtle, but still life-limiting structural racism. The evidence and outcomes of that can be seen in the ways that British citizens who are black are disadvantaged in housing, health, education and the criminal justice system. Similarly, Marvin Rees, a former mayor of Bristol who is involved with the Repair Campaign, says, “Individuals today are not responsible for their ancestors’ wrongdoings. It is, however, important to make a link between individuals and institutions. Individuals inherited institutions and institutions bestowed advantages.”
Arguments that position reparations as a subject of the distant past are overlooking the facts. UK taxpayers have been paying back the colossal sum that compensated the owners of enslaved people after the Abolition Act 1833 – a bill that was only repaid in full in 2015. It’s not British people who should apologise, but the British government that used taxpayers’ money to compensate those who profited from trading in people.
Because of the legacies of this trade, many descendants of those responsible for transatlantic enslavement are still part of the financial elite of this world. Some of them, like the Heirs of Slavery, are attempting to engage with the question. The UK government should work with families whose ancestors received compensation in 1837 and who are ready to work towards a restorative justice plan – and with institutions such as the Church of England, Lloyd’s of London and universities that have started to do the work. Combining resources is the way forward now.
Black communities who have their life chances negatively affected by systemic racism were also paying the bill for the owners of their ancestors until 2015. So, if the debt to the slavers can endure without question into this century, surely repair for the legacies of ongoing systemic injustices should be dealt with on similar terms.
- 
  Olivette Otele is a historian and distinguished research professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London

title: How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
content_c:
How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
November 3, 2026
"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.
It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.
Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.
This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.
Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.
Inspired by 'imperfect' divas
"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.
Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."
The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.
Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.
This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.
"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."
Building community through drag
Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.
In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.
Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.
Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.
Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.
As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.
That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.
In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.
"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."
Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in." 
"There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.
The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.
description: As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

title: Selenskyj, Merz und der Kampf gegen die Zweifel
content_c:
Krieg gegen die Ukraine Selenskyj, Merz und der Kampf gegen die Zweifel
Auch vor dem fünften Winter seit Russlands Überfall ist ein Ende des Krieges in der Ukraine nicht in Sicht. Kanzler Merz betont, dass er fest an der Seite des Landes steht. Doch nicht nur er merkt, dass immer mehr Überzeugungsarbeit nötig ist.
Berlin kennt sich aus mit Staatsgästen. Wenn ein Besuch angekündigt wird, ohne einen Namen zu nennen, wissen die meisten: Gemeint ist der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj. Kommt er, werden große Teile der Stadt abgeriegelt. So auch diesmal, als die unendlich wirkende Kolonne am Kanzleramt vorfährt. Friedrich Merz erwartet seinen Gast und die beiden gehen über den Roten Teppich, die Hymnen werden gespielt und manchmal von den Hubschraubern in der Luft übertönt.
Dem Bundeskanzler kommt es auf die Bilder an. Es war Merz, der am Vormittag offiziell verkündete, wer in Berlin erwartet wird. Er erinnert an den Besuch Selenskyjs in Washington im Februar vergangenen Jahres, der als Desaster endete. Der Ukrainer wurde vor den Augen der Welt vorgeführt und mehr oder weniger rausgeworfen. Das werde in Berlin anders verlaufen, kündigt der Kanzler an.
Merz: Ukraine-Hilfe in deutschem Interesse
"Lieber Wolodymyr, du hast Deutschland und du hast die deutsche Bundesregierung unvermindert an deiner Seite", sagt der Bundeskanzler in der Pressekonferenz, die mit etwa 30 Minuten Verspätung beginnt. Merz setzt eine zentrale Botschaft und das gleich mehrfach: Der Ukraine zu helfen - das sei in deutschem Interesse. "Wir tun es, weil es für unsere Sicherheit, für die politische und die Friedensordnung in ganz Europa wichtig ist. Ich werbe auch dafür, dass dies die Mehrheit der Deutschen versteht, dass wir dies tun."
Deutschland ist mittlerweile der größte Unterstützer der Ukraine, seit sich die USA unter Präsident Donald Trump mehr und mehr zurückziehen. Das betont der Bundeskanzler - mahnt aber, dass auch andere Europäer Verantwortung tragen. Am 19. November kommt die "Koalition der Willigen" nach Berlin, also die Länder, die bereit sind, zu helfen. Dann werde auch über das Jahr 2027 gesprochen.
AfD und BSW schüren Skepsis
Merz weiß natürlich auch, dass längst nicht alle ihm folgen, wenn es darum geht, die Ukraine zu unterstützen - in der Welt, aber auch zu Hause in der eigenen Bevölkerung. Selenskyj ist noch nicht einmal gelandet, da meldet sich AfD-Chefin Alice Weidel auf X. Die Oppositionsführerin teilt ein Video: Bilder, die zeigen sollen, wie Demonstranten am Stadtrand von Kiew mit der ukrainischen Nationalgarde aneinandergeraten. In einem Gebäude sollen junge Männer festgehalten worden sein, nachdem sie zum Militärdienst rekrutiert wurden.
Zu sehen ist auch ein junger Mann, der angeblich gefoltert wird. Doch an dieser Darstellung gibt es Zweifel und keine unabhängige Bestätigung. Weidel fordert trotzdem, der Kanzler solle mit Selenskyj darüber sprechen. Einen ganz ähnlichen Post setzt BSW-Gründerin Sahra Wagenknecht ab.
Deutschland will am Verhandlungstisch sitzen
Der Bundeskanzler betont, dass er die Deutschen überzeugen will und sagt: "Wir sind auf jeder Ebene darum bemüht, diesen Krieg zu einem Ende zu bringen." Heißt übersetzt: Natürlich geht es auch um Diplomatie. Schon in der kommenden Woche beginnen neue Friedensgespräche in Abu Dhabi - zwischen der Ukraine und Russland unter Vermittlung der USA. Da kann Deutschland nur zuschauen - wieder einmal.
Merz fordert, dass Europa mit am Tisch sitzen müsse, wenn es um einen Frieden gehe. Auch, falls die USA Russlands Präsidenten Wladimir Putin zum G20-Gipfel nach Miami im Dezember einladen sollten. "Es ist jedenfalls aus meiner Sicht völlig inakzeptabel, dass Drittstaaten über das Schicksal der Ukraine sprechen, ohne die Ukraine daran zu beteiligen." Er fordert also, dass auch Selenskyj nach Miami eingeladen wird, sollte Putin zum Gipfel kommen.
Selenskyjs Appell an die Deutschen
Auch wenn niemand nachgezählt hat. Es gibt wohl kaum ein Wort, dass Präsident Selenskyj in Berlin öfter nutzt: "Danke!" Dass ihm US-Präsident Trump einmal vorgeworfen hat, undankbar zu sein, hat Wirkung hinterlassen. Auf der Berliner Sicherheitskonferenz spricht Selenskyj viel über die USA. Ohne Amerika, sagt er, wären viel mehr Menschen in der Ukraine gestorben. Er erinnert an eine USA, die einmal für die Regeln in der Welt einstanden und es schimmern deutliche Zweifel durch, wieviel davon noch gilt.
Die Ukraine werde niemals aufgeben, so Selenskyj. Aber allein könne sich heute kein Land beschützen. Dann sagt er fast flehentlich: "Bitte bewahren Sie Deutschland als ein Land, an das die Menschen glauben können". Die Rolle Europas werde wichtiger. "Und ohne Deutschland ist das unmöglich." Da steht ein Präsident, der ganz offensichtlich spürt, dass auch in Deutschland die Zweifel wachsen.

title: Streik bei öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien in Tschechien
content_c:
Streik bei öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien in Tschechien
3. November 2026
Mit einem Streik protestieren Beschäftigte der öffentlich-rechtlichen Radio- und Fernsehsender in Tschechien gegen die geplante Abschaffung der Rundfunkgebühren in dem EU-Land. Zahlreiche aktuelle TV-Sendungen fallen an diesem Dienstag (03.11.2026) aus, sie werden durch Wiederholungen ersetzt. Der Hörfunk sendet fast ausschließlich Musik.
Zu der eintägigen Aktion haben eine Mitarbeiterinitiative und Gewerkschaften aufgerufen. Sie fürchten nach eigenen Angaben um die Unabhängigkeit des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks. "Wir sind entschlossen, beide Institutionen zu verteidigen und ihr Grundprinzip zu erhalten, nämlich dass sie für euch alle da sind - nicht für die Politiker", heißt es in einer Erklärung.
Nach den Plänen der rechtsgerichteten Regierung von Ministerpräsident Andrej Babiš soll der öffentlich-rechtliche Rundfunk künftig aus dem Staatshaushalt finanziert werden - und nicht mehr über das bisherige System regelmäßiger Gebühren, gezahlt von Privathaushalten und Unternehmen. Ein entsprechender Gesetzentwurf wurde vom Abgeordnetenhaus in Prag bereits in erster Lesung gebilligt.
Kahlschlag im Programm?
Vorgesehen sind Kürzungen der Finanzmittel des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks um mehr als 15 Prozent. Dies dürfte einen Abbau von Arbeitsplätzen, Einschränkungen bei Produktionen und die Einstellung von Programmen zur Folge haben.
Kritiker monieren, dass die tschechische Regierung durch die Reform die Möglichkeit erhalten würde, die Medien unter ihre Kontrolle zu bringen. Sie verweisen dabei auf ähnliche Entwicklungen in der Slowakei unter Ministerpräsident Robert Fico sowie in Ungarn, bevor dort Regierungschef Viktor Orbán im April abgewählt wurde.
Ein Finanzierungsmodell über Steuermittel "öffnet politischem Druck Tür und Tor und bedroht die redaktionelle Unabhängigkeit", warnten die Europäische Journalisten Föderation, die NGO "Reporter ohne Grenzen" und andere Medien-Organisationen in einer gemeinsamen Stellungnahme.
Babiš, der in der Vergangenheit wiederholt öffentlich-rechtliche und andere etablierte Medien angegriffen hatte, bildete Ende vergangenen Jahres eine Regierungskoalition mit zwei kleineren politischen Gruppierungen, die für extremistische Positionen bekannt sind. Zu deren Zielen gehört auch eine Verringerung der Hilfen für die von Russland angegriffene Ukraine.
wa/pg (dpa, ap)
Redaktionsschluss: 17.00 Uhr (MEZ) - dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.

title: Не бекон і не шинка. Дієтологи назвали ідеальне «паливо» для тренувань, яке варто додати до ранкової яєчні
content_c:
Не бекон і не шинка. Дієтологи назвали ідеальне «паливо» для тренувань, яке варто додати до ранкової яєчні
До яєчні з індичкою можна додати ще один інгредієнт — гриби (Фото: NV Food via Chat GPT All)
Звичний бекон чи шинка — не єдиний варіант, який варто додавати до яєчні-бовтанки. Дієтологи радять звернути увагу на інше поєднання продуктів, яке може зробити звичний сніданок ще цікавішим і поживнішим.
Яєчня-бовтанка — це класичний і дуже поживний сніданок, проте її користь для здоров’я значною мірою залежить від того, з якими інгредієнтами вона подається. Хоча традиційне поєднання з шинкою є одним із найпопулярніших і найсмачніших варіантів, дієтологи радять звернути увагу на інші альтернативи, пише El Espanol.
І справді, шинка — це класичне й дуже смачне доповнення, проте фахівці зазначають, що цей м’ясний виріб може містити значну кількість насичених жирів, натрію та штучних консервантів — залежно від конкретного виду продукту.
Приготування шинки разом із яйцями за високих температур призводить до утворення сполук, які з часом можуть зашкодити здоров’ю серцево-судинної системи (особливо за умови частого та надмірного споживання цієї страви). Це нівелює природну поживну цінність і високий вміст білка, які в іншому разі робили б такий сніданок (або прийом їжі) корисним.
Щоб перетворити цю страву на справді збалансований і корисний варіант для будь-якої ситуації, дієтологи радять замінити шинку на курячу грудку. Це пісне м’ясо вирізняється низьким вмістом калорій і жирів, слугуючи чудовим джерелом чистого білка, який ідеально доповнює амінокислотний склад яєць.
Така заміна не лише суттєво зменшує споживання шкідливих жирів, а й допомагає підтримувати стабільний рівень холестерину. Завдяки цьому страва стає ідеальним вибором для тих, хто прагне контролювати свою вагу або покращити вигляд тіла за допомогою тренувань у спортзалі чи інших видів фізичної активності.
Крім того, до яєчні з індичкою можна додати ще один інгредієнт — гриби. Вони надають страві соковитості, компенсуючи низький вміст жиру в пісному м’ясі, а також значно підвищують її поживну цінність, майже не додаючи зайвих калорій.
Гриби багаті на клітковину, вітаміни та калій; вони також містять потужні антиоксиданти, що сприяють зміцненню організму. У результаті така яєчня стає не лише потужним джерелом білка, а й цінним постачальником важливих мікроелементів.
Втім, поєднання яєчні з шинкою не обов’язково є поганим варіантом. Проте вживати її варто помірно й лише час від часу, оскільки вона містить багато жиру та натрію, надмірне споживання яких у довгостроковій перспективі може призвести до проблем зі здоров’ям.
Найкраще те, що така страва на сніданок — чудовий спосіб розпочати день, отримавши заряд енергії та значну порцію високоякісного білка. Це ідеальне «паливо» для ваших тренувань, що допоможе досягти реальних результатів.
Збалансований сніданок: яєчня-глазунья зі шпинатом у "човнику" з батату
Марокканська яєчня з сиром: сніданок, який не набридне
Найсмачніша яєчня, яку тільки можна вигадати: рецепт на сніданок
Правова інформація. Ця стаття містить загальні відомості довідкового характеру і не повинна розглядатися як альтернатива рекомендаціям лікаря. NV не несе відповідальності за будь-який діагноз, поставлений читачем на основі матеріалів сайту. NV також не несе відповідальності за зміст інших інтернет-ресурсів, посилання на які присутні в цій статті. Якщо вас турбує стан вашого здоров’я, зверніться до лікаря.

title: Гренландия сказала «да» Трампу: парламент ратифицировал соглашение с США
content_c:
Парламент Гренландии во вторник ратифицировал соглашение о безопасности, заключенное с президентом США Дональдом Трампом, хотя некоторые представители оппозиционных партий выразили сомнения относительно экономической выгоды от этого соглашения. Об этом сообщает Reuters.
В сентябре Соединённые Штаты, Дания и Гренландия подписали соглашение, призванное положить конец напряженности, возникшей после неоднократных угроз Трампа установить контроль над стратегически расположенным и богатым полезными ископаемыми островом, который является самоуправляемой территорией Дании.
Соглашение расширяет военное присутствие США в Гренландии, открывая путь к созданию двух новых военных баз и размещению системы противоракетной обороны Трампа «Золотой купол». В то же время оно подтверждает суверенитет Дании и право гренландцев на самоопределение.
Большинство депутатов уже выразило поддержку соглашению во время первого обсуждения в прошлом месяце. Во время голосования во вторник 16 депутатов поддержали соглашение, никто не проголосовал против, семеро воздержались.
В январе Белый дом заявил, что Трамп рассматривает варианты приобретения Гренландии, в частности возможность применения американских вооруженных сил. Это вызвало беспокойство европейских правительств и привело к интенсивным дипломатическим усилиям по урегулированию ситуации.
Министр иностранных дел Гренландии Муте Эгеде заявил во вторник, что ратификация соглашения стала важным шагом для острова.
«Мы должны признать, что мир и стабильность больше не являются тем, что мы можем воспринимать как само собой разумеющееся», — сказал Эгеде депутатам в Нууке незадолго до голосования.
Оппозиционная партия «Налерак», являющаяся наиболее заметной политической силой, выступающей за независимость Гренландии, в ходе обсуждения поставила под сомнение экономическую выгоду от соглашения.

content:

В сентябре Соединённые Штаты, Дания и Гренландия подписали соглашение, призванное положить конец напряженности, возникшей после неоднократных угроз Трампа установить контроль над стратегически расположенным и богатым полезными ископаемыми островом, который является самоуправляемой территорией Дании.

title: Трамп розкритикував телеканал Fox News і назвав його опитування замовними
content_c:
Президент США Дональд Трамп різко розкритикував електоральні опитування та падіння рейтингів телеканалу Fox News, охарактеризувавши питання як замовні й звинувативши менеджмент упередженості, написав він у середу.
"Рейтинги Fox News стрімко падають (на 27%!), тому що вони витрачають надто багато часу на висвітлення Демократів... Опитування Fox News, завжди найгірше і є настільки образливими через запитання, які вони ставлять. Кожне запитання – це замовна робота, і кожна відповідь – повна нісенітниця! Це триває роками", – написав Трамп у своїй соцмережі Truth Social.
За словами політика, падіння інтересу глядачів до телеканалу зумовлене їхньою позицією проти нього, а власні електоральні показники серед республіканців він назвав найвищими в історіі.
Раніше, коментуючи виданню CBS News шанси на перемогу в електоральних перегонах, політик заявляв про наявність хороших перспектив на успіх за умови уникнення негативних результатів.
Як повідомлялося, у вівторок американці вирушать на виборчі дільниці, щоб проголосувати на проміжних виборах до Конгресу США.

title: Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
content_c:
Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
- Published
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.
  - Published26 October

title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
content_c:
What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
- Published
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting.
Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings.
Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe.
Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people.
What are interest rates and why do they change?
An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it.
The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.
The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%.
When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up.
The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation?
The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting.
Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025.
It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026.
Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026, up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices.
The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally.
- What is happening to UK prices? 
  - Published21 October
What is expected to happen to UK interest rates?
At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April.
However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed.
Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.
UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently.
Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year.
- What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? 
  - Published28 September
- Why are UK fuel prices rising again? 
  - Published2 October
How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates?
Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey, external.
About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.
Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans.
An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.
But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are.
Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in the rates being offered.
As of 3 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.97%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.
The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%.
About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply.
Mortgage calculator
You can see how your mortgage may be affected by future interest rate changes by using our calculator:
Credit cards and loans
Bank of England interest rates also influence the amount charged on credit cards, new bank loans and car loans.
Lenders can decide to raise their own interest rates if Bank hikes make borrowing costs more expensive.
Equally, they can cut their own rates if Bank cuts make borrowing cheaper.
Savings
The Bank base rate also affects how much savers earn on their money.
A rising base rate is likely to mean an increase in the returns offered to savers by banks and building societies and vice versa.
As of 3 November, Moneyfacts said the average rate for an easy access savings account based on a balance of £10,000 was 2.56%. The average rate for an easy access cash ISA was 2.77%.
The average rate for customers who were prepared to lock their money away for a year was 4.47%.
Changes in rates particularly affect those who rely on the interest from their savings to top up their income.
What is happening to interest rates in other countries?
In recent years, the UK has had one of the highest interest rates in the G7 - the group representing the world's seven largest so-called "advanced" economies.
In June 2024, the European Central Bank (ECB) started cutting the main interest rate for the eurozone from an all-time high of 4%, falling to 2% in June 2025.
However, in June 2026, the ECB raised rates to 2.25% as it reacted to the Iran war, before raising them again to 2.5% in September.
The US central bank - the Federal Reserve - raised rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting, the third under the new chair Kevin Warsh.
It meant rates rose to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75%, following three cuts since September 2025.
US President Donald Trump had repeatedly attacked the previous Fed chair Jerome Powell for not cutting rates.
Warsh said the rise was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".
After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

title: Spanish transport minister resigns after deadly train crash
content_c:
Spain’s transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday after the train crash that killed 69 people last week, one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
Óscar Puente, who had earlier pledged to work “tirelessly” to restore confidence in the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, also said he was withdrawing from the country’s upcoming general election.
Last week’s crash, and another disaster earlier this year, have overshadowed campaigning for the 29 November ballot, in which the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, is trailing in opinion polls.
Puente had ruled out resigning on several occasions since the disaster.
But at the end of a lengthy hearing before lawmakers, he said: “I wish to inform you that I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but that I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections on 29 November.”
Hours earlier, at a press conference during which he presented measures to improve safety, the minister had said the government would “work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public’s trust in high-speed rail”.
The rightwing opposition, which had demanded Puente’s resignation, and unions had criticised him for appearing to pin all the blame for the disaster on one control centre operator.
The crash happened when a train operated by the state-owned company Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish operator Iryo on Wednesday outside the village of Urda, about 80 miles south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 39-mile stretch of track, but a control centre nonetheless authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey.
Among the measures announced at the earlier press conference by Puente was the creation of software for control centres that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot anomalies in traffic.
Puente said an AI agent would be created to oversee the system and “minimise the possibility of human error”, describing the proposal as unprecedented.
In scenarios where a control centre operator took a decision while the automatic safety system was down, a second operator would have to confirm it, Puente added.
The train drivers’ union Semaf, which has called strikes at Renfe for 10 and 12 November, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of “degraded systems”.
Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalisation of Spain’s rail network, which allowed private companies to break Renfe’s decades-long monopoly.
In an apparent recognition of the unions’ demands, Puente said the working conditions of control centre operators would be reformed, including their breaks and by monitoring their fatigue levels.
Puente also announced an aid package of €30m (£25m) for the families of the dead and the scores of people who were injured in the crash.
Another collision in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same key line connecting Madrid with the city of Seville, Spain’s first high-speed route when it opened in 1992.

author: AFP in Madrid
content:
Spain’s transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday after the train crash that killed 69 people last week, one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
Óscar Puente, who had earlier pledged to work “tirelessly” to restore confidence in the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, also said he was withdrawing from the country’s upcoming general election.
Last week’s crash, and another disaster earlier this year, have overshadowed campaigning for the 29 November ballot, in which the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, is trailing in opinion polls.
Puente had ruled out resigning on several occasions since the disaster.
But at the end of a lengthy hearing before lawmakers, he said: “I wish to inform you that I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but that I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections on 29 November.”
Hours earlier, at a press conference during which he presented measures to improve safety, the minister had said the government would “work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public’s trust in high-speed rail”.
The rightwing opposition, which had demanded Puente’s resignation, and unions had criticised him for appearing to pin all the blame for the disaster on one control centre operator.
The crash happened when a train operated by the state-owned company Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish operator Iryo on Wednesday outside the village of Urda, about 80 miles south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 39-mile stretch of track, but a control centre nonetheless authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey.
Among the measures announced at the earlier press conference by Puente was the creation of software for control centres that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot anomalies in traffic.
Puente said an AI agent would be created to oversee the system and “minimise the possibility of human error”, describing the proposal as unprecedented.
In scenarios where a control centre operator took a decision while the automatic safety system was down, a second operator would have to confirm it, Puente added.
The train drivers’ union Semaf, which has called strikes at Renfe for 10 and 12 November, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of “degraded systems”.
Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalisation of Spain’s rail network, which allowed private companies to break Renfe’s decades-long monopoly.
In an apparent recognition of the unions’ demands, Puente said the working conditions of control centre operators would be reformed, including their breaks and by monitoring their fatigue levels.
Puente also announced an aid package of €30m (£25m) for the families of the dead and the scores of people who were injured in the crash.
Another collision in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same key line connecting Madrid with the city of Seville, Spain’s first high-speed route when it opened in 1992.

title: Shabana Mahmood has barely softened her plans – Britain’s immigration regime is now a theatre of cruelty | Owen Jones
content_c:
Five years ago, Shabana Mahmood called for a “general amnesty” for undocumented migrants. “That’s not official Labour party policy yet,” she mourned, “but myself and a group of other Labour MPs are continuing to make the argument.”
Now home secretary, she is introducing one of Europe’s most punitive immigration and asylum systems. The standard qualifying period for migrant workers to gain secure residence will double to 10 years, which will be twice the length set out in almost all EU countries. The standard wait for refugees who claim asylum in Britain outside designated resettlement routes will be 20 years, four times the usual five-year qualifying period in Germany, Spain and Italy.
But even this is misleading. As the Home Office notes: “There are no visa routes to enable people to claim asylum in the UK from overseas.” As it further adds: “A person must be present in the UK to claim asylum here.” So accessing this punitive process by regular means is in essence impossible.
Mahmood has reopened an exceptionally limited resettlement scheme, with Afghan women and girls and Palestinians expected to account for about a quarter of referrals. The latter is a shamelessly cynical sop to progressive voters infuriated by Labour’s complicity in Israel’s genocide. And previously exceptions have been made for travel to Britain for humanitarian reasons: from Ukraine, Hong Kong and Afghanistan. But if you’re seeking to flee persecution in, say, Iran, Eritrea or Somalia, you cannot legally apply for asylum. Arriving by small boat is your only shot. For those who do and have their asylum claims accepted, a wait of up to 30 years for permanent residency beckons.
Eleven years ago, Mahmood spent three days at a refugee camp in Greece and wrote about her experiences in the New Statesman. “You would run,” she told her readers. “I would run. They are running. We must do our part to help them.”
Bear in mind that Britain receives fewer asylum applications per capita than the EU average. Bear in mind, too, that nearly seven in 10 of the world’s refugee population are hosted by low- and middle-income nations. Remember also the role of Britain in violence that has caused destabilisation and accelerated population movements – such as the wars in Iraq and Libya, the latter of which Mahmood voted for.
Yes, there has been a partial retreat on social care workers, with those who entered the route before May 2025 and meet the relevant conditions able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. But consider how the social care sector has already been plunged into crisis by Britain’s “cut off its nose to spite its face” immigration policies. New international recruits plunged from 105,000 to 30,000 in the space of two years – while the sector has nearly 100,000 vacancies. Mahmood’s concessions will not reverse that crisis.
Here is why these policies are such a travesty. The fundamental breach of trust is a violation of any principles of natural justice. When Mahmood’s Conservative predecessor Theresa May introduced a £35,000 settlement salary threshold in 2012, she exempted migrants who had obtained qualifying work visas before April 2011. Mahmood, on the other hand, is applying the 10-year baseline to many of those already lawfully resident. That’s despite many migrants and their families having made plans around what was promised to them. Half a million people will be hit by this promise-breaking.
What of the rampant classism of someone who earns more than £125,000 qualifying in only three years, while someone below £50,000 normally waits 10? The New Economics Foundation once released research that found that a childcare worker generated up to £9.50 of social value for every pound they were paid; a hospital cleaner created £10; a recycling worker produced £12. A City banker, on the other hand, destroyed £7 of social value for every pound they generated; that was £11 for an advertising executive and £47 for a tax-avoidance accountant. But these exorbitantly paid occupations have a three-year pathway, compared with 10 years for underpaid crucial workers.
Mahmood has at least recognised that nurses, teachers and care workers offer contributions that cannot be captured by salary alone. But why doesn’t this principle apply to other workers?
Then there’s the supposed party of labour undermining the collective bargaining power of workers by keeping them dependent on employer-sponsored visas for a decade. Even the Home Office has admitted that settlement can improve wages because workers have the freedom to change jobs. These plans will damage migrant and British-born workers alike. “This creates downward pressures across sectors as a whole,” the Trades Union Congress notes, “as sponsorship impedes workers’ ability to campaign for better pay and conditions or fight back against poor treatment.”
Then there’s requiring migrants to have gone five years without accessing specified state support before qualifying for settlement on the standard route, or face a longer wait – although the exact scope and exemptions are not yet clear. People with disabilities could be punished, while parents may be forced to impose hardship on their children in order to gain permanent residency.
All of this is based on a pernicious lie that both media and political establishments have promoted in Britain: that immigration is responsible for our country’s problems. Not the financial sector, which plunged the country into a disaster from which we have never recovered. Not greedy exploitative bosses not paying their workers properly after the labour movement was permanently hobbled in the 1980s. Not an economic order rigged in favour of Big Finance and assets instead of productive industry, or politicians who won’t build the housing we need. No, it was migrants who became the scapegoat.
Well, now that a hostile environment has well and truly been constructed for migrants, who will the scapegoaters have to blame?
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist
-

title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
content_c:
Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
November 3, 2026
In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.
He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.
But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."
Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.
For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.
It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.
The nonalignment years
The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.
In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.
Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.
This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.
EU membership
Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.
Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.
The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.
The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.
Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.
Close relations with Moscow
The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.
The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.
The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.
Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.
These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.
Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
Turning point in 2022
The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.
"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.
Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.
The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.
Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.
Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.
What form does the rapprochement take?
The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.
Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.
An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.
The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.
Cyprus and NATO
The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.
The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.
At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."
Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."
Phasing out Russian weapons
The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.
After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.
The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.
Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).
The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
description: The Republic of Cyprus long balanced ties between Russia and the West. Now, it is phasing out Russian weapons, expanding defense cooperation with the United States and redefining its place in the Eastern Mediterranean.

title: Google blockiert Suchfunktion, wenn Schulen KI ablehnen
content_c:
Software für den Unterricht Google blockiert Suchfunktion, wenn Schulen KI ablehnen
Google zieht gegenüber US-Schulen die Daumenschrauben an. Verbietet eine Einrichtung in ihren Räumen die Nutzung künstlicher Intelligenz, will das Unternehmen den Schülern künftig den Zugriff auf die Google-Suche sperren. Ein Zugriff auf die Suchfunktion sei nur möglich, wenn sich die Schule ausdrücklich für den Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz entscheide. Das teilte der Technologieriese am Dienstag mit.
Immer mehr Pädagogen, Kinderentwicklungsexperten und Eltern sehen es kritisch, wenn Schüler im Unterricht die neuesten Google-Tools nutzen. Die Skepsis hat sich noch verschärft, seit das Unternehmen im August bekannt gab, dass es seinen KI-Chatbot »Gemini« für viele Schüler in den USA freigeschaltet hat, die die Unterrichtsplattform Google Classroom nutzen.
Am Dienstag erklärte das Unternehmen, Schulverwaltungen würden Googles KI-Funktionen nicht mehr automatisch freigeschaltet bekommen. Stattdessen könnten Schulen jedes Google-Tool einzeln aktivieren oder deaktivieren, darunter den KI-Assistenten Gemini, Gemini Notebook und die Suche. Jedes Tool sei standardmäßig deaktiviert, bis die Administratoren es einschalteten. Da die Suche jedoch in die KI integriert sei, verlören Schulen, die sich vollständig gegen KI entschieden, auch den Zugriff auf die Google-Suche.
Google verspricht lernfreundliche Antworten
»Wir sind der Meinung, dass Schulen die Kontrolle über KI in ihren Klassenzimmern haben sollten und dass wir den Schulverwaltungen Steuerungsmöglichkeiten an die Hand geben müssen, die ihnen bei der Gestaltung ihres Ansatzes helfen«, schrieb Chris Phillips in einem Blogbeitrag . Er leitet als Vice President den Bildungsbereich bei Google.
Das Unternehmen teilte außerdem mit, es aktualisiere seine Suchtools, damit sie »lernfreundlicher« würden. Unter anderem sollen Schüler keine schnellen Antworten auf ihre Schulaufgaben erhalten. Eine vollständige Deaktivierung der KI sei jedoch nicht möglich, wenn Schulen Google-Produkte nutzen wollten.
Google ist der dominierende Anbieter von Bildungssoftware an US-Schulen. Weltweit nutzen laut Unternehmensangaben 150 Millionen Schüler und Lehrer die Plattform »Google Classroom«. Viele Schüler verwenden zudem Chromebooks, die ihre Schule bereitstellt.
Kritik an »Zwang zu KI«
Im August geriet Google in die Kritik, als es seinen Chatbot »Gemini« auch für jüngere Schüler freischaltete. Bis dahin hatte Google die Aktivierung von Gemini nur für Personen ab 18 Jahren zugelassen.
Pädagogen, Pädagoginnen und politische Entscheidungsträger kritisierten die Ankündigung vom Dienstag. »Google nutzt sein Suchmonopol, um Schulen zur Einführung von KI zu zwingen«, schrieb Lina Khan, ehemalige Vorsitzende der Federal Trade Commission auf X.
Dies zeige die Gefahren, wenn man einem unregulierten Monopolisten die Kontrolle über einen systemrelevanten Dienst überlasse. »Während sich die Öffentlichkeit zunehmend gegen den Einsatz von KI in Schulen wehrt, macht Google deutlich, dass es diejenigen bestrafen wird, die sich nicht fügen.«
Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service.

New York City und Los Angeles hatten vorübergehende Verbote für generative KI-Tools in Grund- und Mittelschulen erlassen. Sie prüfen den Einsatz und bewerten die Sicherheit von KI und wollen Richtlinien für deren Nutzung entwickeln. Experten hatten zudem Bedenken geäußert, dass der Zugang zu KI der Gehirnentwicklung von Kindern schaden könnte.

Software für den Unterricht Google blockiert Suchfunktion, wenn Schulen KI ablehnen
Google zieht gegenüber US-Schulen die Daumenschrauben an. Verbietet eine Einrichtung in ihren Räumen die Nutzung künstlicher Intelligenz, will das Unternehmen den Schülern künftig den Zugriff auf die Google-Suche sperren. Ein Zugriff auf die Suchfunktion sei nur möglich, wenn sich die Schule ausdrücklich für den Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz entscheide. Das teilte der Technologieriese am Dienstag mit.
Immer mehr Pädagogen, Kinderentwicklungsexperten und Eltern sehen es kritisch, wenn Schüler im Unterricht die neuesten Google-Tools nutzen. Die Skepsis hat sich noch verschärft, seit das Unternehmen im August bekannt gab, dass es seinen KI-Chatbot »Gemini« für viele Schüler in den USA freigeschaltet hat, die die Unterrichtsplattform Google Classroom nutzen.
Am Dienstag erklärte das Unternehmen, Schulverwaltungen würden Googles KI-Funktionen nicht mehr automatisch freigeschaltet bekommen. Stattdessen könnten Schulen jedes Google-Tool einzeln aktivieren oder deaktivieren, darunter den KI-Assistenten Gemini, Gemini Notebook und die Suche. Jedes Tool sei standardmäßig deaktiviert, bis die Administratoren es einschalteten. Da die Suche jedoch in die KI integriert sei, verlören Schulen, die sich vollständig gegen KI entschieden, auch den Zugriff auf die Google-Suche.

Er leitet als Vice President den Bildungsbereich bei Google.
Das Unternehmen teilte außerdem mit, es aktualisiere seine Suchtools, damit sie »lernfreundlicher« würden. Unter anderem sollen Schüler keine schnellen Antworten auf ihre Schulaufgaben erhalten. Eine vollständige Deaktivierung der KI sei jedoch nicht möglich, wenn Schulen Google-Produkte nutzen wollten.

title: Spanien beschließt nach Zugunglück neue Sicherheitsmaßnahmen im Bahnverkehr
content_c:
Neue Sicherheitsmaßnahmen Spanien zieht erste Konsequenzen aus Zugunglück
69 Menschen starben vor knapp einer Woche bei der Kollision zweier Hochgeschwindigkeitszüge - es war bereits das zweite schwere Zugunglück in Spanien in diesem Jahr. Nun sollen neue Maßnahmen die Sicherheit verbessern.
Knapp eine Woche nach dem Zugunglück mit 69 Toten hat die spanische Regierung Maßnahmen zur Verbesserung der Sicherheit im Bahnverkehr beschlossen. Zudem sei ein Hilfspaket von 30 Millionen Euro für Opfer und Angehörige gebilligt worden, teilte die Regierung von Ministerpräsident Pedro Sánchez mit. "Wir versichern, unermüdlich daran zu arbeiten, das Vertrauen der Öffentlichkeit in die Hochgeschwindigkeitszüge wieder herzustellen und zu erreichen", sagte Verkehrsminister Óscar Puente.
Zwei Hochgeschwindigkeitszüge waren am Mittwoch vergangener Woche nahe der Gemeinde Urda südlich von Madrid zusammengestoßen. Ein Zug der staatlichen Bahngesellschaft Renfe fuhr von hinten auf einen stehenden Zug des privaten Betreibers Iryo auf. Es war das zweite schwere Zugunglück innerhalb von nur neun Monaten in Spanien - im Januar waren bei einem Zusammenstoß zweier Hochgeschwindigkeitszüge in Adamuz in Andalusien 46 Menschen ums Leben gekommen.
Zugsicherungssystem und Kontrollzentrum im Fokus
Während im Fall von Adamuz u. a. ein Gleisbruch als Ursache gilt, konzentrieren sich die Ermittlungen zum Unglück in Urda vor allem auf den Ausfall des Zugsicherungssystems LZB und mögliche Fehler im Kontrollzentrum des Netzbetreibers Adif. Bisherigen Erkenntnissen zufolge soll ein Mitarbeiter nach einem Ausfall des Leitsystems falsche Anweisungen gegeben haben.
Die Zahl der Züge zwischen Madrid und Sevilla solle nun so lange reduziert werden, bis dort das neue europäische Zugsicherungssystem ERTMS in Betrieb gehe, erklärte Puente. Fällt das bisherige LZB-System aus, muss zudem künftig ein zweiter Mitarbeiter im Kontrollzentrum die Anweisungen an die Lokführer überprüfen und bestätigen. Damit soll verhindert werden, dass Züge trotz unklarer Streckenverhältnisse weiterfahren.
Darüber hinaus sollen die Personalstärke in den Kontrollzentren erhöht und die Arbeitsbedingungen der Mitarbeiter verbessert werden. Die Regierung beschloss auch Preisobergrenzen für alternative Verkehrsmittel während der Sperrung der Unfallstrecke, um überhöhte Kosten für Reisende zu verhindern.
Alle Todesopfer identifiziert
Das Hilfspaket umfasst direkte staatliche Hilfen, Vorschüsse auf spätere Entschädigungszahlungen und eine Verdoppelung der Leistungen aus der gesetzlichen Fahrgastversicherung. Opfer und ihre Angehörigen sollen über eigens eingerichtete Anlaufstellen betreut werden. Für Verletzte ist zudem eine besondere Regelung zur vorübergehenden Arbeitsunfähigkeit vorgesehen.
Knapp vier Wochen vor der vorgezogenen Parlamentswahl in Spanien steht die Minderheitsregierung von Ministerpräsident Sánchez wegen des Zugunglücks massiv in der Kritik. Die Opposition fordert nach dem zweiten schweren Zugunglück in diesem Jahr personelle Konsequenzen.
Alle 69 Todesopfer des Unglücks - 40 Männer und 29 Frauen - wurden inzwischen identifiziert, wie die Behörden mitteilten. 37 der insgesamt rund 200 Verletzte werden noch in Krankenhäusern behandelt.

title: Ukraine-Krieg: USA bringen Moskau und Kyjiw an einen Tisch
content_c:
Ukraine-Krieg: USA bringen Moskau und Kyjiw an einen Tisch
3. November 2026
Trotz andauernder Angriffe keimt wieder Hoffnung auf, dass neue Verhandlungen zwischen Russland und der Ukraine den Weg zu einem Ende des Kriegs ebnen könnten. Vertreter aus Moskau, Kyjiw und Washington würden sich kommende Woche für zweitägige Verhandlungen in Abu Dhabi treffen, teilte der US-Sondergesandte Steve Witkoff mit.
Die Dreiergespräche sollen den seit Monaten stockenden Friedensbemühungen neuen Schwung verleihen, so Witkoff. Die Vereinigten Staaten würden die Verhandlungen auf Arbeitsebene "moderieren". Damit werde die "Mission" von US-Präsident Donald Trump zur Beendigung des fast fünf Jahre andauernden Kriegs vorangetrieben. In dem Format hatte es zuletzt im Februar in Genf Verhandlungen gegeben.
Im Zentrum der Gespräche sollen laut Witkoff "Sicherheitsvereinbarungen für die Zeit nach dem Krieg, Deeskalation, humanitäre Maßnahmen sowie weitere Schritte auf dem Weg zum Frieden" stehen. Noch vor den neuen Verhandlungen in der Hauptstadt der Vereinigten Arabischen Emirate würden die US-Unterhändler in Brüssel auch mit Vertretern aus Europa und der NATO zusammenkommen, kündigte der amerikanische Sondergesandte an.
"Müssen Druck auf Russland ausüben"
Die internationale Gemeinschaft müsse Russland klarmachen, dass Terror nicht akzeptiert werde, forderte abermals der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj. "Wir müssen einen solchen Druck auf Russland ausüben, dass es keine Alternative hat, als diesen Krieg zu beenden." Konkret verurteilte der ukrainische Staatschef einen russischen Luftangriff auf das Dorf Komyschuwachain der Region Saporischschja, bei dem es am Montag zahlreiche Tote gab. Die Attacken hätten auf eine Schule abgezielt, die zu "humanitären Zwecken" genutzt worden sei.
Mit Blick auf Geheimdienstinformationen warnte Selenskyj zudem vor massiven russischen Angriffen während der Kongresswahlen in den USA. Auf der Onlineplattform X erklärte Selenskyj, die Aufmerksamkeit der ganzen Welt werde sich auf die US-Wahlen konzentrieren, "und was in der Ukraine passiert, inklusive unserer Schwierigkeiten bei der Luftabwehr und mit Patriot-Raketen, wird nicht wahrgenommen".
An diesem Dienstag kam Selenskyj zu einem vorher nicht angekündigten Besuch nach Berlin, wo er von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz empfangen wurde. Deutschland ist mittlerweile der größte Unterstützer der Ukraine in deren Abwehrkampf.
Zuletzt nahm Russland nach Angaben aus Kyjiw vor allem wieder die Energieinfrastruktur der Ukraine ins Visier, aber auch ein Krankenhaus in der Großstadt Charkiw. Russland meldete ebenfalls neue ukrainische Angriffe. So seien in der Nacht zum Dienstag Hunderte Drohnen auf Moskau zugesteuert, berichtete Bürgermeister Sergej Sobjanin im Onlinedienst Telegram.
"Koalition der Willigen" übt in Polen
Von Montag kommender Woche an werden in Polen rund 2800 Soldaten aus elf Ländern am ersten Militärmanöver der "Koalition der Willigen" zur Unterstützung der Ukraine teilnehmen. Dabei solle getestet werden, wie nach Kriegsende ein dauerhafter Frieden gesichert werden könne, teilte das britische Verteidigungsministerium mit. Großbritannien und Frankreich leiten die Übung "Koalicja 2026" (Koalition 2026), die bis zum 22. November laufen soll. Auch Deutschland beteiligt sich mit Stabsoffizieren, Tankflugzeugen und Logistik.
Das Manöver der Multinationalen Truppe für die Ukraine (MNF-U) sei ein "wichtiger Meilenstein", erklärte der französische General Armel Dirou. Sie stelle "konkret unter Beweis, dass die MNF-U unmittelbar nach Ende von Kampfhandlungen einsatzbereit ist". Parallel dazu findet unter türkischer Führung von Istanbul aus eine maritime Simulation statt, um die Einsatzbereitschaft für mögliche Minenräumaktionen im Schwarzen Meer zu testen.
wa/pg (dpa, afp, rtr)
Redaktionsschluss: 17.00 Uhr (MEZ) - dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.
description: Im zähen diplomatischen Ringen um ein Ende des russischen Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine könnte es bald etwas Bewegung geben. Die Multinationale Ukraine-Truppe konzentriert sich bereits auf die Friedenssicherung.
